Your examiner has duly examined the petition of C. M. Mr. SPROULE I think it would be really advisable to let this stand over for a day that we may have an opportunity to look into it, because there is much about it not present to one's, mind in looking over it hurriedly and for the first time. speechtext: There is no objection from anybody. This Bill, like all other Bills which are submitted to the House, will receive a reasonable consideration.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee on Bill (No. 6) to amend the Criminal Code.
On section 1,

I only intend to take up but a short time in discussing this Bill, as I am anxious, like every one else, to reach a settlement. I believe a compromise may be reached which will be satisfactory to the country, and which ought to be satisfactory to both parties in the House. If the compromise proposed last night by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. McColl) is accepted, we will have in this country less than 100 days of racing where now we have over 250 days. We will have the hand-book eliminated and made criminal, we will have tipsters' advertising and tipsters' offers of information prohibited, we will have the advance information in the pool-room prohibited, and the time for racing will be reduced from 250 days to less than 100. Then we will have an opportunity in the next few years of seeing whether that does not substantially reduce the abuses that now exist. I wish to draw attention to the issue as it exists in this country. While you may by this legislation be stopping betting, you may stop racing by stopping betting, and if you stop racing you are not going . to stop betting. That is clear to my mind. It has been attempted before, it has been attempted in other states to stop betting by prohibiting racing, and the attempt has failed. Where such Bills have been passed in the states, betting still continues, only it moves in another circle where you cannot control it as well as you can now. To my mind, this measure will he absolutely futile in the object of stopping betting. Betting is more or less inherent in humanity, people will find a way of betting and, of all forms of betting, that which should be stopped because it is the most scandalous is the betting on the stock exchange. There is far more money lost, there is far more injury done to the public and they have a poorer chance for their money in betting on the stock exchange than in betting with the book-makers on the race-track.
Will this Bill not reach the stock exchange?
I do not know whether this will reach the stock exchange or not.
No, no.
Who says ' no? '
I do.

I am quite sure that this Bill will not stop betting, but it is possible in every British community to regulate any evil. There is a betting evil in this country-we all admit that-there is a betting evil in connection with race-tracks, and the way to meet that evil, and to minimize it, is to regulate it and not attempt to abolish it. We do know that the most satisfactory treatment of the. drink evil is the regulation of the drink traffic, and in Ontario and the different provinces twe have, not prohibition, which han been found a failure, but we have the regulation of the drink evil which is a success, and under that regulation the drink evil is being gradually minimized. It is on those lines that we should approach this evil of racetrack betting and we should minimize it by putting under regulation the conduct of race-meetings controlled by men who take an interest in racing, on its merits, and an interest in stock breeding, and that regulation would best be effected by the amendment of the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. McColl). While you stop racing, as you do by this sweeping law which is now before the House, you do it at the expense of horse-breeding. I thoroughly agree with the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) in his contention last night that an injury is done to the breeding of horses by the stopping of racing. I have represented in past years the constituency in which the Woodbine race-track is located. I have known a good deal about racing and horse-breeding in the country, and I absolutely agree with the evidence and the statement of the hon. member for *Brandon, that horse-racing in some way, is necessary for the maintenance of the thoroughbred horse, and that the thoroughbred horse is the greatest asset in connection with racing horses and the horse industry in this country. I am not going to enlarge upon it. I have had a wide enough experience of it to know-although I do not know what the reason is and nobody can account for the anomaly-that the perpetuation of the thoroughbred horse does tend to carry on the qualities of endurance and stamina which are the ground work of all the lighter breeds of horses. All the good military horses, whether chargers, or cavalry horses, absolutely derive their stamina, endurance and courage from the thoroughbred horse and the more thoroughbred horses we have in this country the better able we are to provide good horses for. the army of the empire and our own militia forces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And thoroughbred men.

And thoroughbred men. The country that has done that Mr. CONMEE.
most effectively is Great Britain. Their horses are the "best in the world, and they are taken all over the world for military and breeding purposes. Horse-racing is a very old British institution. It has been identified with British life hundreds of years, and it has never been a crime in England-and a great many of our people come from the old land-to bet with the book-makers at race-meetings. In some way horse-racing and the breeding of the thoroughbred are at the bottom of British character. All through British literature you will find these things mingling the world over, and they are represented as the real things at the foundation of British character. There is a love of the country, there is a love of thoroughbred animals, a love of live stock, a feeling of chivalry and military prowess in the British character that in some way is identified with horses and in some way is maintained by horsebreeding and the traditions that go with it. The things that have carried the Britisher wherever he has gone have been his military prowess, his chivalry, and his devotion of horse-racing and sport. These have been at the foundation of British character. It is no new thing-this desire of the British people 'to give race meetings, or to find sport in race meetings and betting on horses. It is almost as old as British character itself, and it runs through all our literature. Through the general literature of the entire world, in some way, there is a regard for horses and a desire to be associated with horses and identified with chivalry, military prowess and things of that sort. The desire of the ordinary British citizen to go to race meetings, to see contests between horses and to bet on horse-races is a part of the British character, and I do not see why we should interfere with that desire ir. the way that is proposed in this legislation.- The Britisher values above all things his liberty of personal conduct and he resents the attempt o'f somebody else to interfere with it. Wherever he has gone, in Australia, in Canada, in South Africa, in India, the Englishman has taken his racing instincts with him, he has taken racing there and he has done nothing of which he ought to be ashamed, but, on Mie contrary, he has maintained those underlying features of British character which are the strength of British character and British government throughout the world. So, this proposition to do awaj7 with horse-racing, to prevent people from going to the races and betting occasionally upon a race involves the placing of a stigma on British character and on things that are at the foundation of it. I happened to know the men who were identified with the starting of the Ontario Jockey Club. They were men of high character. They recognized the fact that

the British public must have sport, that the British public is essentially a sport-loving public and men like the late Mr. Hendrie, the late William Christie, the late Sir Casimir Gzowski, and the late Charles Brown, and the late T. C. Patteson, who established the Ontario Jockey Club had no desire other than to see British institutions and traditions maintained in this country through racing with which they had been identified. They recognize that the public had to have racing and they were willing to take charge of racing in Toronto and to give the public good clean . sport of that kind. They succeeded in giving it. The finest social gathering and the most characteristic gathering to-day in all Canada is that which you wall see at the Woodbine race track during the spring and fall meetings. This is essentially a representative Canadian meeting. It is a meeting of the best collection of men and women that I have ever seen at any place in Canada and to bring within tiie Criminal Code by this legislation now before the House those gentlemen who established racing in Canada and those people who go to the Woodbine race track, Toronto, is to stigmatize the very best citizens of this country who are simply living up to the traditions of their race, to their rights as British subjects and are doing nothing criminal -whatsoever that I can see. It is a pretty hard thing and a thing to be considered with some care, this going out of one man to make a rule of life for his fellow, to stigmatize anything that he thinks he does not agree with and to put that fellow within the Criminal Code The greatest manifestation of the strength of British political character to my mind in so far as our government is concerned, was in what we call the puritan or the presbyterian, or, if you like, the Protestant idea which developed in England many years ago. This- idea was the absolute freedom of the individual, his freedom of conscience, his right not to be dictated to by any one, and the right to make the rule of life for himself. As long as the puritan idea was political, and maintained that lib-erty-things were all right. And the puritan did another thing, he applied his self-denying ordinances to himself, and as long as he did that he was the greatest force in politics, and in morals. But the moment the puritan proposes to make the rule of life for some one else, for you, for me, he transgresses, he abnegates the great position he has, and he becomes somewhat of a tyrant. The strength of British character is shown when the puritan idea is political, and maintains its great principles, when the puritan idea manifests itself by self-control, and self-denial, but the moment it abandons that, and undertakes to regulate the personal conduct of others, it
has failed. That is at the bottom of what is happening in this country. A number of people outside of the cities where racing is carried on are asking for this legislation. The cities have not petitioned for this, one-seventh of the population of Canada is in the cities where racing takes place and not a call comes from any of these cities. In other words, outside places are undertaking to dictate the rule of life to the rest of the people in regard to their personal conduct on race-tracks. That is not liberal, that is not British, and, as the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) said yesterday, there is no moral sanction for any such law when an attempt is made to put it in force in a British country, and you must have a moral sanction behind a law if you wish to vindicate that law.
Is my hon. friend aware that within the last two weeks a meeting of 400 young men of the city of Toronto at which Sir William Mulock was chairman, passed a standing resolution in favour of this Bill?
That may have been so, but that is not from the citizens of Toronto.
From 400 of them.
If they had wished for this we would have heard it here, and I challenge the hon. gentleman, if he wishes to advance this Bill, to bring the people here.
Toronto's opinion is no criterion.
Toronto is a criterion for its own conduct.
Is the hon. gentleman aware that the grand jury

Yes, I am aware of what the grand jury did. What the hon. gentleman wants to do, and is at liberty to do is to regulate his own conduct, and make the law of life for himself, but I wish to be free as a British citizen to make my own rule of conduct, and not to be interfered with in it.
In order to show where the American character begins to differentiate from the British I may say that in the United States they are attempting to abolish betting on race-tracks. It became such a scandal that the legislature had to intervene, and that interference took the drastic form of abolishing it. That course has not succeeded. But there is this difference between the American character, and the British character. In the British character there is a love of liberty, and British institutions are a success. There is a failure in personal liberty in the United Stales, and the result is that American institutions are called

into question. I read a book last year by Captain Lee on * The Ignorance of Valour,' and the whole lesson of that book is that the Americans no longer have the fighting quality, that if they were to go to war with Japan to-morrow the Americans would be defeated, because they have lost their love of liberty, and largely their military prowess. I have here an extract from another American who has been in England, and studied British institutions. This book is by Mr. Price Collier, and is entitled ' England and the English, from an American point of view.' It is one of the ablest books on the English character, and the condition of things in England that has been written in many years. Mr. Collier is forced to admire the conditions of affairs in England. He says:
Sitting on the bench at Bow street with the magistrate, I listened all one morning to his disposal of the cases that came before him. It seemed to me when I left that I had known beforehand what would happen. Quarrelsome women and men, mostly through drink; men and children accused of begging; a few cases of assault or resistance to the constable; all of them, hour after hour, dealt with in a good-tempered, paternal sort of way, with appeals to their own sense of what was right. Only the cases where there had been resistance to the constable who represents British law and order, then hard labour and wholesome punishment.
Here is the point:
Always the same from the King to Bow street. How can we live together amicably, with the utmost freedom for each one? that is the problem. The practical result is-you see it if you have eyes, everywhere you go- a success.
Englishmen are at all times trying to livb together and to give each other the greatest freedom and they do give one another the greatest freedom from the King down. Any one in England can go on a race-track and be doing nothing immoral; he need expect no interference from any one else. But we are setting up the doctrine in Canada that in some way it is our duty to interfere with the personal liberty of one another, and exercise some kind of surveillance one over the other. As the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton^ said last night, if that is started in this country, if we commence passing such legislation in this House, putting the conduct of one another within the Criminal Code, where is the end? Let us respect the liberties of one another, and maintain those liberties; let us maintain most of all those personal liberties which we have. That ought to be the end and aim of our life in this country, to afford liberty and not to afford restriction. There is nothing to-day that forces any man to go to a race-track and bet.. People must learn self-control, and if anybody is unfortunate in going to race-Mr. W. F. MACLEAN
tracks he ought to blame himself rather than the law. We ought to educate our people, our young men especially, to avoid betting and control themselves so that they will not fall into such a trap. If a master finds a clerk addicted to race-track betting, he ought to discharge him or speak to him instead of seeking legislation. Betting is good for no one, but if an individual wishes to make a bet on a race-track in connection with a meeting he is attending, I say he is doing nothing immoral, nothing unBritish. and there is no reason why his conduct should be stigmatized as being illegal or criminal. In the United States they are confessing a lack of military prowess and confessing that in some way Japan may defeat them if they should go to war, and they are trying to improve character by putting restrictions on it, while at the same time the great public rights and liberties that should be maintained are disappearing, and a government by monopoly worse than any government by aristocracy is growing up in that country. Private rights are going, public rights are going, but the tyranny of the great trusts and corporations is growing, yet at the same time they are trying to stop horse-racing, which is one of the simple amusements of the people.	.
I shall not take up much more time but may speak a little later on the various propositions as they come up, but I wish to impress if possible both those friendly to the Bill and those opposed to it that a compromise is the way out of the situation. We can reduce races to less than a hundred days in Canada, we can abolish the attendant evils, and then see the result of the experiment. If in the next three or four years the evil of betting, under the proposed amendments, should become flagrant, we may then bring it under the Criminal Code, hut I do not think that will be found necessary. I believe in regulation and not in prohibition, and under the proposed amendment, two great interests will not be destroyed as they would be by the Bill of the hon. member for Grey. If that Bill should be adopted, the horse industry would be injured and those who invest money in racing would stand to lose, and a great public sport would be legislated out of existence. There will besides be a disposition on the part of a great many in this country to regulate the conduct of others. I would not like to see anything of that kind. What we require is to preserve personal liberty in every possible way. If there be any grievance, regulate it, but preserve personal liberty, because personal liberty is the foundation of the British character and the secret of the strength of British institutions. When a drastic measure is nroposed, when it is proposed to stigmatize a large and re-

spectable section of the community as criminals, there ought to be some kind of moral sanction established to justify that interference, there ought to be some strong public opinion that the thing aimed at is immoral and criminal. I do not know that public opinion is ready to stigmatize the attendance at a race-track as a criminal practice. That is not the case in England. The first gentleman in the empire has been quoted as in some way condemning race meets. I would like to see the hon. member for South Grey quote anything from the eminent personage to show that he was against horseracing or to betting as an incidental in connection with it. Let me refer to the  * opinions of another eminent Englishman Lord Rosebery, but before doing so I shall read another short extract from 'Collier's' work on England and the English.
The English common sense comes to the fore again in an attempt to solve this problem. She is old enough to know from experience that the world is still ruled by men, and in all probability will be for a long time to come. She breeds men therefore as strong and simple as she can. In these islands sport is not a dissipation for idlers, it is a philosophy of life. They believe in it as a bulwark against effeminancy and decay.
There is the very statement I was making a short time ago. The Englishman believes in sport as a bulwark against decay and effeminancy. The Duke of Wellington said that Waterloo was won on the Eton cricket ground. The English military reputation has been attained by men which w'ere fond of the horse and addicted to sport. Let me vive an incident in connection with Lord Rosebery:
A Congregational minister makes a speech in which he confesses to ' a feeling of bitter humiliation ' when he reads that the Prime Minister is the owner of a Derby winner, and stands to. win or lose thousands of pounds on the race. Lord Rosebery's attention having been called to this speech by a political opponent, he replies as follows: 'Sir, I am desired by Lord Rosebery to thank you for your letter and its inclosnre. He will offer no opinion on the latter, for these matters should be dealt with according to good taste, Christian charity, and knowledge of facts possessed by each person who touches on them.' The letter is signed by the Prime Minister's secretary.
According to Lord Rosebery, Christian charity should be exercised, and we ought not to attempt to stigmatize a man because he happens to own a race-horse and attend a race-meet.
Lord Rosebery is one of the most accomplished Englishmen of the day; he considers it lacking in Christian charity to abuse him for owning and breeding a great race-horse. So do probably more than nine out of ten of his countrymen. From top to bottom of English society, from the Prime Minister to the
Yorkshire footballer, sport is almost as much a part of the national existence as eating and drinking.
If there be an evil in connection with sport, let us get rid of it by regulation. And if you regulate horse-racing, as proposed in the amendment, you will introduce nothing improper and do no wrong, and you will not stigmatize decent people as coming within the Criminal Code. I resent the insinuation that my fellow citizens of Ontario, and especially Toronto and the surrounding district, are to De stigmatized and put within the Criminal Code.

Does my hon. friend understand that book-making is in the Criminal Code? He says that every one connected with horse-racing in Ontario is stigmatized by the provisions of this Bill. To whom does he refer?

First of all there are my fellow citizens of Toronto who belong to the jockey club. The hon. member from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) is on the executive of-that club, so is a senator in the other House. , There are other gentlemen on its executive, and who actually bet on the race-track, and if the hon. gentleman's Bill should carry these will be stigmatized as doing something illegal and immoral. Every one who goes on a racetrack is stigmatized as guilty of an immoral act. Every one who goes to a race-meet will be so stigmatized.

No.
Mr. w' F. MACLEAN. Yes, especially any man who wishes to bet

I do not so understand the Bill. The only prohibition in the Bill is against the book-maker, not against the bettor. There is no pretense to stigmatize ttie private individual who chooses to bet. The sportsman who goes to a race and finds another sportsman to bet with him is at liberty to do so. What is made criminal is the book-maker and no ont else.

On the contrary, eminent personages in this country have been held up to the people as guilty of moral wrong because they attended the Woodbine. I say there was nothing wrong in that. I have no sympathy with people who undertake to make a rule and law of conduct for others. There is a way of reaching this thing as an evil, and I hope to hear an explanation from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) regarding that letter of his which was read here yesterday. There is a way by which each province can regulate these things. Certainly making acts innocent in themselves criminal is not the way to accomplish anything, and I hope this House will not begin the work of undertaking to regulate the

personal conduct of individuals. I appeal to the common sense of the House not to begin this work, but to maintain and preserve personal liberty. Let every man make a rule of life for himself. There is no compulsion on people to go to race-tracks and bet, and there is no reason why their personal liberty should be interfered with, either as regards attending or refusing to attend r-aee-meets. I have had some experience in Ontario of this attempting to make the law of conduct for other people. Take the instance of the Sunday street cars, which excited so much hostility, but which resulted in the people at last winning the right to travel on Sunday. We were then told that we were doing something immoral, that public opinion was against us, that the cars should not be allowed to run on Sundays under any circumstances. but the public will finally gaiip its end. What we ought to have is not tyranny, but regulation." So I appeal to the common sense of the House to regulate race-meets and not abolish them. I appeal to the House not to interfere with property and private interests, and with such a great industry as" horse-breeding.

STRATTON (West Peterborough) I had intended last evening making a few observations, but on account of the abrupt way in which the debate closed, I did not feel it was desirable to detain the House at that time. This question has been before the country for a considerable time. I have listened to the speeches of those opposed to this measure; and giving these gentlemen all the credit for the ability they have displayed, which was very great, in my opinion they have been inconsistent in the arguments they put forward. When an hon. gentleman" says that public opinion is not in favour of this Bill, I desire to take issue with him. When the hon members for Brandon (Mr. Sif-ton) and West Northumberland (Mr. Mc-Coll) pointed out that public opinion is not in favour of this Bill, I desire to dispute that statement; and I venture to say that my hon. friend who has just sat down (Mr. Maclean) cannot name five newspapers in Ontario which are opposed to the principle of the Bill. On the other hand, I can name dozens which have urged the adoption of this measure, because it is in the right direction, and because great evils have grown up under the present law. My hon. friend from West Northumberland (Mr. McColl) referred to the thieves and other doubtful characters who attend the Toronto and similar exhibitions. Let me point out that the Attorney General of Ontario sends to such large gatherings detectives and others to protect the public. But if the amendment be adopted the very reverse will be the case. The hon. gentleman desires, as far as race-tracks are con-Mr. W. F. MACLEAN
cerned, to legalize the very causes which attract thugs and thieves to the race-tracks and public exhibitions held from time to time. He referred to the fact that the bookmaker, would be in the same class as the dangerous characters referred to as frequenting large gatherings, so far as access to large assemblages of the public would facilitate the opportunities of his plying his admittedly nefarious occupation. The opponents of the Bill, in the proposed amendment, seek to aid and, if it prevails, will legalize bdbk-making on the race-course. It will license him, it will protect him, while the Bill proposes to do away with the bookmaker, and thus protect those, unable from lack of knowledge or experience of the snares set for them, to protect themselves. Horse-racing, as conducted in Ontario today, can be altered and improved, and a new method adopted by which horse-racing will not be interfered with, but the root of all the evil, the book-maker and book-making, will be abolished. I do not desire to interfere with racing, or the development of the thoroughbred, but I do not believe that it is at all necessary for that purpose to have book-makers on the race-track to rob the public, to contribute to the racing associations, and furnish the purses to be given on the pretext of developing the thoroughbred horse. I do not believe that is at all necessary and consequently I am opposed to any compromise that will have the effect of perpetuating book-making. New York state was referred to by my hon. friend from West Northumberland (Mr. McColl). He pointed to the conditions now existing there and the loss of prestige of the thoroughbred horse owing to the abolition of legalized gambling. Well, there may be a loss of prestige temporarily, there may be a diminution in the value of the thoroughbred as a racer, but there is no reduction in the actual value of the thoroughbred, that I know of, in the state of New York at present. It is not often we look across the line for precedents, but, if we should do so in this case, we would find that the state of New York is not thinking of abolishing their law, but of amending and improving it, so as to make it even more effective than it originally was.
During the Easter vacation I was in New York and took occasion to ask-not the goody goody people, as they are sometimes termed-but men of business whom I met in the financial world-I took occasion to ask them as to the result of the operation of the Hughes law. I asked them was it the goody goody people that were particularly responsible for the passage of that Act. I was informed to the contrary, that of course their moral support was with the Bill, but that the business houses and financial institutions that gave their

support most earnestly to the adoption of the Hughes law were those whose influence was behind its adoption; and it was further stated that those who were previously giving their attention to the race-track and losing their money, were now paying their debts, butchers' bills and rents more promptly than they ever did before. If that be the case across the border I think these conditions could be imitated on this side of the line to advantage.
My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) went on to make a comparison between gambling at the race-track and betting on an election. I do not think there is any comparison between the two. If a man desires to make an innocent bet, on the result of an election to show his faith in the candidate of his party, he has all the previous conditions surrounding the candidate to guide him. He is not held up by the book-maker, but banks on his own judgment, founded on his knowledge of the popularity of the candidates, and the local conditions.
If he desires to bet upon that question he is backing up his political faith. Also, he has an opportunity of judging of the merits of the candidates and of the questions and issues before the people. Making an ordinary bet, he makes it under conditions entirely different from those which face the average citizen who goes to the race-track and makes his bet with the book-maker, for that average citizen has but little chance of winning. The hon. member compared the making of a bet with a book-maker and the purchase of stock with a stock-broker. I think there is no comparison whatever. If a man goes into a broker's office and buys stock, he gets what he pays for. He may be mistaken in his judgment as to the value of the stock, or he may buy more than he is able to take care of. But it is only when he fails to pay his debts that the wrong comes in or an injury is done to any other person. The hon. member also referred to life insurance. Again. I say, there is no comparison whatever. The man who takes out life insurance gets -what he pays for. The amount is paid to his heirs at his death or to himself at the maturing of the policy, as the case may be. In either case, he has paid for what he gets, and he gets no more than he has paid for. It is true, as one hon. member said early in the debate. that there is more or less of a chance in any business occupation upon which a man may enter. If a man takes up the drygoods business he may make a mistake in the quantity, quality or selection of the goods he buys. But in every business a man has an opportunity to exercise his own judgment and in making a purchase, he gets what he pays for. Not so when he deals with a book-maker on the race-track.
My hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Sif-tonV spoke of what he called the peculiar
method adopted for the promotion of social reform as evidenced in this Bill. The hon. member quite approved of the action of parliament in passing the Lord's Day Bill of a few years ago. But I would ask him to point out any single difference of principle between that measure and this. One is in the interest of the public, and so is the other, and if the Lord's Day Bill is right, there is no doubt, in my opinion, that the present Bill is right also. The hon. member (Mr. Sifton) spoke of the thoroughbred horse and its importance to the farmer, and he also mentioned, if I remember right, the Ottawa association as one that had afforded the farmers in the neighbourhood special opportunities for the improvement of their stock by the use of the thoroughbred horse. We know thkt the farmer does not use the thoroughbred horse to any great extent, and, if what the hon. member says concerning the Ottawa association be correct-and, of- course, I fully accept what he says on that subject-it only shows a desire to create in the farmer's mind an impression that the thoroughbred horse can be useful to him. The hon. member for Brandon also said that confiscation of property was involved in the passing of this measure. If there be a confiscation of property in the difference between 10 per cent and 10,000 per cent on the stock of these racing associations, then there may be an appearance of confiscation. But I contend that there is no real confiscation of property by the adoption of this measure. While there may be a depreciation to some extent in the value of a few of the thoroughbred horses throughout the country, there is no other confiscation that can be so recognized. This parliament, or any legislature, does not hesitate for a moment to amend the law affecting any business, but bases its legislation simply upon considerations of the public interest. And nothing is said against their so doing. If the parliament of Canada can reduce to a minimum the evil of book-making from one end of this country to the other by the adoption of this measure, I believe they will be doing something that will be in the right direction, something for which they will have every reason to expect the approval of the overwhelming majority of the people.
My hon. friend from West Northumberland (Mr. MeColl) has proposed an amendment. the effect of which would be to legalize race-track gambling in its entirety. He would give to race-track associations a monopoly of the betting on horse-racing in this country. And. while my hon. friend from South'York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) is willing to extend the privileges to those who are able to attend tbe race-meets of the Ontario .Tockev Club in Toronto, yet bis regard for liberty of action and of speech is not sufficient to cause him to

Under the Bill of my hon. frienl from South Grey, he would not be able to carry on private betting to any considerable extent, but if this amendment is adopted it is sufficiently wide to enable

book-makers to do all the business they desire to do. I think that would be found to he the case, and that they would be able to drive a coach and four through this Bill, as they have done in the case of other legislation. Again the amendment says:
Any constable may take into custody, without warrant, any person found committing an offence under this section, and may seize and detain any article liable to be forfeited under this Act.
You might as well say that any constable *on the Kingston road may take into custody, -without warrant, any person, because if the person is carrying on betting outside, then he can be taken and carried off unceremoniously to prison. That is what my hon. friend advocated a moment ago. But if the individual is inside the track, if he has the advantage of the law so that he may get inside the racing inclosure, then he is free and is at liberty to carry on betting to the fullest extent. I am absolutely opposed to the amendment I think it kills the principle of the Bill, and I think the desire of the House is that we should adopt the principle of the Bill. I think it is the duty of this parliament to afford the people the protection to which they are entitled. We are not interfering with the rights of anybody further than is necessary in the public interest, even though the Bill went to the fullest extent desired by its most ardent supporters. I believe it should be adopted, and that by doing so we would be meeting the wishes of the vast majority of the people of Canada. I care not whether the Bill has been advocated by the Lord's Day Alliance, or by certain clergymen, or whether petitions have been sent in. We do know that this House was flooded with petitions at the commencement of the session. We are all able to judge of their value. But for us to say that there is no public sentiment in favour of the Bill is a mistake, and any hon. gentleman will deceive himself if he entertains that opinion. There is a strong public sentiment in favour of it, there is a strong feeling throughout the country that something should be done to protect the innocent, to protect those who are unable to protect themselves. I wall not quote to you the remarks of clergymen with regard to gambling upon the race-track; but I think that one of the most powerful sermons ever delivered against race-track gambling was the opinion expressed by the famous Silent Smith who died in Pittsburg a year or two ago, and who had accumulated about $3,000,000 in gambling. This is what he said on his death bed:
Race-track gambling is as insidious as the most powerful drug, gradually developing as if the victim was not strong enough to resist the temptation. Few people have the ability
to be successful on the track. The best evidence he could give of that was that he could count on the fingers of one hand those men who, in the past century, had made money out of race-track gambling.
He said further that:
He would welcome the laws that would prevent the youth of the land spending money and energy in following the ponies.
So, we have from one who followed the race-track for years, who knew what the advantages, and disadvantages of it w'ere, and w'ho made large sums of money for himself in connection therewith, this dying statement. This parliament has a duty to perform in the interest of the youth of the land, and that is to. adopt legislation which wall guard them from the risks that are surrounding them in connection with racetrack betting. One of the greatest horse figures in the United States-Keene, who spent more money upon his horse stables than perhaps any other man in the world, over half a million a year, made a statement upon this subject, and what did he say? Betting is not necessary to horseracing and that he had never placed a bet on a horse. The Agnew Bill in the state of New York is being backed up by the public sentiment of the- state, and the opposition to this Bill which has only developed is being worked up by those who are particularly interested in opposing that legislation, just as an effort Is being made to create a feeling around this building hostile to this measure, because it is claimed that it will interfere with the development of the thoroughbred horse. I do not believe anything of the kind. I believe that the thoroughbred horse will be fostered just as successfully in the future as he has been in the past because the evidence that came before the committee showed conclusively that that development had not been as rapid as could have been desired especially in view' of the alleged benefits of fifty years racing in Canada, and evidence of which w'as the fact that when the Boer w'ar broke out they could not obtain in Canada the quality ' and quantity of horses that the British army required. For my part, I am in favour of the measure now before the House, and I hope that the parliament of Canada will see its w'ay to place upon the statute-book a law that will give protection to our citizens, and that protection which is absolutely essential. If other countries can adopt legislation such as this, the parliament of Canada should meet the wishes of the people in so far as this measure goes, and I believe that by adopting this Bill it will be meeting the wishes of the people.

(Translation). Mr. Speaker, before dealing at length with w'hat wras said in the course of yesterday's debate as to the sub-

ject now under discussion, I may be allowed to briefly refer to some statements just made by the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Stratton). The hon. gentleman expressed an opinion as to the usefulness of the thoroughbred. He acknowledged in passing that he did not know very much about the matter. That was apparent, that was evident. I take his word when he says that he has no extensive knowledge as regards the thoroughbred. Farmers, he says, are not fond of the thoroughbred. Of course they are right in preferring another type if they want a horse only to hitch to the plough or to draw heavy loads. In that case, I would agree with the hon. gentleman and admit that for such work the thoroughbred is not suitable. But, there is some other use to which the thoroughbred can be put on farms; and I speak advisedly when I say so. To back up that statement I have my own personal experience covering twenty-five years, during which I have had the pleasure, not to say the advantage-as it comes rather high-of taking an interest in farming matters, and I invite the learned members to visit my stables, wherein he will find thoroughbreds of some value.
The farmer, it is said, has a dislike for the thoroughbred, I have just stated the reason. However, in order to make myself clear. I shall further say that the thoroughbred is useful for the improvement of heavy breeds of horses, such as the Ardennais, the Hackneys, the Normans, and the Per-cherons. We even have to-day Brabansons which are too* slow, too heavy to be profitably put on the road. But the Brabansons, as well as the Percherons and the Normans, are great breeds of horses which should be improved, made lighter by crossing them with the thoroughbred.
The thoroughbreds are small, it is urged. Yes, but they are full of stamina; and when desirous of improving our heavy draught breeds, we are very careful to cross' them with thoroughbreds which are the mearis of bringing about a happy medium, that is of breeding horses which can be used on the roads or in the fields without breaking through, as do the Norman, the Percheron. or the Brabanson. Whenever such heavy horses have to be put to work in the fields before the surface is settled down, they injure the sod in meadows and pastures by sinking knee deep into the ground, and besides they are liable to break down fences and gateways, while the thoroughbred goes clean over them without causing any damage.
In the province of Quebec the ' National Breeders' Association ' offers fine stallions which have cost a good deal of money. Henceforth, we have no use for any others. On the other hand the owner of a thoroughbred mare which has been imported Mr. LAFOETUNE.
at considerable cost, will not breed that mare to a thoroughbred, but to a horse of a heavier type, so as to obtain a progeny which may be of service at all kinds of work, whether on the road or in the field. Besides, they may occasionally be sold at high prices, on account of the qualities developed in them by judicious breeding. Such is my answer to the hon. member for Peterborough who has just stated that we have no use for the thoroughbred.
Formerly we dispensed with automobiles, with electric traction, telephone and telegraph lines and even railways. That recalls to my mind an old-timer in my constituency who was averse to the building of a railway line to Montreal; of course that line was built in spite of his opposition, but he would never travel by it, because it had been built by Liberals. He persisted in using exclusively his old grey nag. Those are errors of judgment, exaggerations unworthy of attention. But when we are met by a man who proposes legislating on the lines inidicated and inserting in the Criminal Code a provision such as we find in the Bill under discussion, it is up to us to call a halt.
I have had the honour of being Crown prosecutor for some years past, in the largest judicial district of the province of Quebec. Well, since I have been acting in the above capacity, taking a hand in the administration of justice, especially in connection with criminal cases m Montreal, for a few years back not a single case, not a single complaint of the character referred to has been brought up in court. The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) stated last evening in my hearing that, while attending the sittings of the police court in Montreal last autumn, he had been struck by the large number of arraignments. Well, I may say to that gentleman that at any of the sittings he might witness a similar condition of things; but these arraignments are not the outcome of the racing going on at the Jockey Club or at Delorimier park. Presently I shall give the names of the people making up the Montreal Jockey Club and the De-lormier Park Association, and the House will be surprised to find that the list comprises men of the highest standing and perfectly well posted as regards proper administrative methods and public morals.
There are crimes in quite sufficient numbers definied by the common and the statutory law and entailing various penalties; and when I hear the hon. member for Grey requesting the House to still add to ti c list of criminal offences and prohibit racetrack betting, it is time that a stop be put to such legislation.
It is quite useless for him to come to Montreal and proclaim such principles, or to call public meetings in the hope of obtain-

ing support. I understand he succeeded in getting together in Toronto four hundred young men, without any experience of life, ignorant of what is in the best interest of the country, and even that has been effected^ only by means of much publicity. I am' surprised that more people should not have responded to the call in that fine city of Toronto, Canada's queen city, as it is sometimes called, though improperly to my mind. That shows that the Bill is not a popular one, for in our province whenever a popular measure is being discussed, instead of four hundred boys, thousands of people will congregate.
The hon. member has made reference to public opinion. Well, I have lust stated what is going on in Montreal. I live in close proximity, within the county of Jacques Cartier. I regret that the member for that constituency (Mr. Monk) who has a great concern in that question, is away.
I hope he will be back before this debate is over, otherwise, when he appeals to his constituents at the next election, we shall make it a matter of serious reproach for him. He is very well posted and has had a long experience in these matters, and no doubt he would have seconded the amendment which the committee has under discussion. His absence then is the more to be regretted on that account.
Is the hon. gentleman aware that the member for Jacques Cartier is seriously ill, and that his absence has no other cause.

I was not aware of that, and must apologize. I hope he will soon recover, and come back in good health and good disposition.
I was just saying, Mr. Speaker, that the Montreal Jockey Club has its grounds in the county of Jacques Cartier, within the limits of the finest parish in the province, that of St. Laurent, where I have my home. That association has spent up to date a million dollars on its race track. I was proud last autumn, when the opening took place under the patronage of His Excellency the Governor General, to witness the assembling there of more than one hundred thousand people. What a fine sight it was! The best and finest people in the province were in attendance, and in particular beautiful women. And everything went on without any unpleasantness whatever. Notice, Mr. Speaker, that as is always the case, perfect order reigned throughout. There are policemen on the grounds who have an eye on strangers coming and going; as regards the Montreal people, who are all good citizens, such measures are unnecessary; but in order to ensure greater safety, and lest some one might act improperly, the association have policemen on the grounds in sufficient numbers
to prevent or counteract any wrong doing.
It is a day of rejoicing for the farming community; it is a festival of agriculture. Before long, I shall request my leaders to set apart a day as the festival of agriculture, ' farmer's day.' No such day has yet been set apart. Professional men, labour men, have their day; the farming community alone is without a day set apart in honour of their calling, which is the finest under the sun. That request I shall not make just now, but at the next session, and mind you it will have to be granted. I let that stand as a notice of motion for next session.
The hon. gentleman's reference to public sentiment recalled to my memory certain utterances of our opponents on another question. They stateu that public opinion was entirely against us and would bnna about our downfall. As evidence, they pointed to petitions bearing a great many signatures and laid before the House.
I cannot say very much about the petitions in favour of this Bill. I do not know what signatures they bear, but what I do know is that very often such petitions are signed injudiciously, by routine without paying any attention at all, and more than anything else; to please the person who takes the petition around. Several of the petitions which were sent with reference to the Naval Bill had been forwarded from my constituency. On looking into them, I found that the signatures were all in the same handwriting. I made inquiries from several of my friends who answered, ' We never signed our names to that petition.'
' But,' I would say, * I saw your names on the document.' ' Well,' they would answer,
' it was put there by my son, my daughter or my wife.' Of late, when people made inquiries to me about the Miller Bill, they would ask: ' Mr. Lafortune, is that Mr. Miller who is circulating a Bill for the purpose of sending every body and soul to jail, the same man wanted to prevent trains from circulating on Sunday? '-' I do not know, but they read pretty much the same.' ' Is he the same man who wished to prevent us from going out on Sundays -' I do not know, but it looks like it; the principles involved are alike.'
If we were to insert in the criminal code provisions against all those who are guilty of wrong-doing, what great number of lawyers and judges would we not need! Even now it is a difficult matter to secure judges for the settlement of business and other lawsuits of importance. Indeed, many judges would be required to dispose of criminal cases, should we undertake to put a stop to all abuses, wrong-doing and to restrain all those who live beyond their means. That might give me a chance of being appointed a judge before long.

No, public opinion is sounder than that; public opinion has matters of greater importance with which to concern itself. I do not wish to be in any way offensive or disrespectful towards the learned gentlemen who support the Bill. But let me say this to them: You should, it appears to me, in the interest of the country, in th.e interest of your electors, busy yourselves otherwise than originating new criminal offences. Crimes are not like mushrooms which develop in the course of a few hours. New crimes should not be imagined in connection with everything. Otherwise, what shall prevent you from legislating against betting on lacrosse grounds. Young men who attend lacrosse matches, who bet large sums on baseball or hockey matches, should also in that case be called to account, prohibited from attending such games, or spending their money in such fashion. Then, why should they not be restrained from going to the theatre, where they have to disburse from five to ten dollars when in compatoy with young ladies? All such expenditure is objectionable. Then, would it not be proper to prevent people from providing themselves with automobiles! Formerly, carts were the great means of travel, while nowadays rubber tires are considered a necessity. If I were permitted to speak out, I would take the right hon. Prime Minister to task for having promoted the welfare of the country. After all, he is to blame if people spend so much today; people are in a position to spend on account of the general prosperity aijd instead of being surprised at the spending of a few dollars on the race tracks, one should express astonishment were the contrary to occur.
I heartily concur in the remarks made by the hon. member for York (Mr. Maclean). Possibly it is the first time that I agree with him, but I hope it will not be the last. Come along and Join in with us, Mr. Maclean, join in with the Liberals who are opposed to these proposals which you rightly condemn.
It is urged that the inserting of this clause in the Criminal Code will not in any way affect the race-track. Well, let us see how it would work out in the case of the Montreal Jockey Club, for instance. There are one hundred thousand spectators assembled on the grounds. On a sudden, ten or twelve policemen appear at the meet and proceed to make arrests. You may be sure that racing will not be continued very much longer. Tumult, trouble, a stampede possibly will ensue. The wives and daughters of those attending will feel uneasy; children will take fright. They would be the first to say: Let us no longer go to see the races to be witnesses of such squabbles and excitement. You may be sure that under such circumstances racing Mr. LAFORTTTNE.
would .soon be a thing of the past; race meets would be abolished.
Evidently, these hon. gentlemen have never been on the race-track. At any rate, they have never attended race meets; or they would have been highly gratified at the way things are managed and amusement provided for them. Mr. Speaker, at recess, I was contending that public opinion which our learned opponents are representing as being on favour of this Bill, is rather in my humble opinion, opposed to it. Public feeling cannot lend itself to giving effect to such personal views in regard to restricting individual freedom, whose defenders those learned gentlemen profess themselves to be.
Let us not interfere with individual liberty. It is an entirely different matter when we are called upon to legislate concerning trade, for instance, or any other matter relating to society in general. Thus when the government submitted an Act in regard to Sunday observance, it was a general law, applicable to all provinces and to all classes of society. However, many persons took exception to that measure as being an encroachment on individual liberty. The majority of the House declared that law necessary; but people went so far as to try to nut a stop to amusements within the family circle and to prevent young people from indulging in moderate, honest and intelligent relaxation. However, that Act for the better observance of the Lord's Day had its good points, and I was, favourable to the principle ol the law, although I did not approve of its rigour.
But in the present case, as I listened to the learned gentleman who preceded me (Mr. Stratton) pointing out as he did to the impoverishment of families through losses sustained by many on the race-track, 1 was tenanted to turn around and ask; What about those who gamble on stocks? What about those who buy stock' which is never delivered to them? What about those business places where numbers of our y.oung men speculate on stocks, and ruin themselves and oftentimes their families? You do not propose introducing legislation with a view to restricting such transactions. And I heard the hon. gentleman stating; There is no comparison possible between gambling on stocks and gambling on the race-track. Well, I think he is right in stating that there is no comparison possible between the two, inasmuch as stock gambling is much the worse evil of the two. Those who go in for betting on the race-track are not guilty of one-hundredth part of the wrong-doing for which gamblers in stock are responsible. Nevertheless, should there be introduced to-morrow a Bill to prohibit stock gambling, that
hon. gentleman would be the first to protest and say: You are encroaching on individual freedom, you are interfering with trade and every day transactions. I might victoriously reply to that hon. gentleman that there is no comparison possible. The farming community, those who take an interest in farming and particularly those who go in for breeding, have a right to the protection of the law. It is contended that this Bill will not interfere with the breeders' business, with the farmers' opportunities. Whereupon I answer to my learned friends that they are astray in their contention that by prohibiting what is now being carried on in an honest, regular and rational way, the breeder's business, which is of interest to us, will not be interfered with.
Wherever racing is being carried on, betting should be allowed, and if betting between individuals only is allowed, and no middlemen permitted to take in the bets, what will become of the money put up in bets? I have some experience in this connection, and I say that if you do away with book-making, you render betting impossible. The money put up in betting will go into the hands of strangers, of irresponsible people, and when the meet is over, it will be found that they are flown. In order to recover the money, recourse to the law courts will be necessary, and a great deal of trouble will be in sight. Betting under such conditions would not be possible, all must agree as to that. Whoever has any experience at all in sporting matters will not say otherwise. As is well known, owners of race-tracks farm out the privilege of book-making to specialists and that is a fair and legitimate way of providing the funds to be given out in prizes.
What was it that induced thousands and thousands of people to gather for last autumn's race meet at Montreal? What was it that drew there 1,500 horses, a good number of which were from across the boundary? What was it, if not the prizes that were offered? Do you think a man in Philadelphia, or New York-there were even one in Los Angeles-would spend large sums to send horses to these race meets, if the stakes were only small sums? Even then, these race horse owners should not be looked at in the light of mere speculators; they send their horses at a loss. They do so for the benefit of the farming community, and in most cases they get only a very small proportion of their outlay. Is f.t fair that such men be subjected to the treatment meted out by this Bill? They spend large sums to promote the breeding of horses on right lines, and the farming community is benefited thereby. I trust, therefore, that the House will sound the death knell of that Bill and will turn down the proposal of these gentlemen,

whose only concern is to originate new criminal offences, and that we will hear nothing more of such theories.
Sir, no good reason can possibly be put forward in support of these contentions. Some latitude should be granted to human nature in selecting amusements, and these cannot be had free of cost. In the same way, the acquirement of learning does not go without fees. Those who attend race meets an engage in betting, acquire experience and that has to be paid for. From what these hon. gentlemen say, one might infer that all are losers at that game. Surely, there must be winners, and who are are they? Book-makers get rich, it is claimed. Of course there are winners in that class, but there are also losers. The money I lose in bets goes into the pockets of the_ fellow who bet against me, barring the amount of a commission of ten per cent generally, which goes to the middleman. That is all the profit the latter gets out of the bettors. On the other hand, the book-maker, who is a dealer in bets, a buyer and seller of bets on the horses listed to run, is himself a loser occasionally. He sells 'horses for first, second or third place, and that horse may come out last, in which case we immensely enjoy taking in his dollars, which you may rest assured, we have no thought of returning to him the day following.
I 'hear the hon. member for Prescott state that the book-maker is not often disappointed. I infer from it that the hon. gentleman has never been on a race-track. Let him come to our meet and he will find out that everything is done honestly, that there is no fraud.
Hon. gentlemen seems to think that there are no means devised towards protecting the individual and putting down abuses. But legal gentlemen who are well up in the knowledge of civil rights and iproce-dure, should not lose sight of those enactments specially designed to protect the individual, whether he be a young man or a father of family, against his own excesses in the matter of gambling or drinking. Have we not such a thing as the privation of civil rights and the family council? If it is shown to the courts that so and so is a spendthrift, a gambler at cards, a drunkard,. a too easy-going fellow, a family council may at once ibe summoned and consulted as to the desirability of interdicting the gentleman and providing him with a curator or judiciary council, whose duty it will 'be to prevent him from extravagant spending. Now it is proposed to have this parliament take the matter in hand and deprive of his civil rights the spendthrift, the gambler, the prodigal. Well, I protest against parliament assuming jurisdiction in matters of this kind. I say parliament has not the right to brand Mr. LAFORTUNE.
any one as a prodigal before his relatives have had their say in the matter. I say that such a course would be an encroachment on individual liberty. I say you have not the right to deal with Canadian citizens as if they were spendthrifts, and restrain their freedom of action without conforming to the rules of procedure enacted by the various provinces of the Dominion. Whenever we are called upon to deal w'ith a prodigal, but not of the most pronounced type, we deprive him in part only of his civil rights, by appointing a judiciary council to prevent him from living in an extravagant manner or spending too freely. Such are the means provided by law to restrain improvident and Teckless people.
Sir, the learned gent who preceded me stated-and I was sorry to hear him say so-: in this connection we prefer following the provisions of the United States law, to following those of the British law. We take after the people of the United States; as to the British enactment, as to the legislation in force in the mother country, they say, we have no use for it, Is that sound reasoning ? To my mind it is a criminal offence, a crime which should be made punishable under our laws, a crime of high treason to thus follow the lead of our neighbours, without paying any attention to what is being done in Great Britain. A Mr. Hughes has been mentioned. I am not acquainted with him, though he may be a very honest man. But I prefer following the legislation in force in the British empire. In support of a bad case, people are ant to make use of every means, good or bad. After centuries of British rule, one should know a thing or two.
I listened with pleasure and a great deal of attention to the statements made last evening by the ex-minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton). I have never heard anything more precise and indicative of so great ability and experience. He gave us the whole thing in a nutshell. His arguments are uncontrovertible, and no attempt was made to answer them. The hon. gentleman who hails from those vast territories which are the hope of the Dominion, has Canadian interests at heart. It cannot be said of him that he is a race track gambler or that he has any kind of interest in racing associations. He gave us his word that he never gambled or engaged in betting, and nobody will doubt his word. His opinion should be given still greater weight, seeing that it is wholly disinterested.
Reference has been made to insurance policies, and the hon. gentleman who made such reference contended that the policyholder gets back only what he paid. Such is not always the case. The policy-holder is not always in that position, as I shall endeavour to show. Take for instance the

case of a life insurance policy. The policyholder dies after having paid his first premium and his heirs get a considerable amount of money which the company is bound to pay. Then take the case of a fire insurance policy. The owner of the building insures it for a large amount. The next day, the building is destroyed by fire, and he gets a lot of money, after paying in a small premium only. Will it be contended that in such cases the insured gets back merely what he had disbursed? However such agreements are considered legal, although they imply a contingency, although their outcome is uncertain, hazardous, in the same as with race-track betting. You bet on a horse expecting he will come out first, and very often he comes out last. You are the loser, but some one else is a winner.
My learned friends spoke of the usefulness of the thoroughbred. It is a well known fact among farmers and breeders generally, that thoroughbreds are high-priced horses. They are not plentiful, require much training, and cost a great deal to their owners. On the other "hand the latter expect to obtain a handsome price for them.
Within the last twenty years governments have spent large sums towards promoting breeding. The Minister of Agriculture, agricultural lecturers, co-operative associations, farmers' clubs, agricultural societies have all in turn advocated better breeding methods, and the improvement of live stock, especially of horses. For several years past, a large number of thoroughbreds have been imported to cross with Canadian horses. Thereby, we have succeeded in bringing about a considerable improvement in our breeds of horses. And when these hon. gentlemen contend that it is possible to continue that work of improvement independently of racing, let me answer that, in my humble opinion, that is not possible. Neither is it possible to provide for the upkeep of a race-track solely by means of entrance fees an contributions forthcoming occasionally from individuals or agricultural associations in connection with the meets. That has been attempted in every county throughout Canada. The idea is not a new one. An effort was made at large agricultural fairs to run the show by means of entrance fees alone, and to be content with a few races comprising only a small number of entries, but that always resulted in a failure. On the other hand, how have matters been improved? Success has been attained by acting in co-operation with the management of large associations. In conjunction with agricultural fairs and ploughing matches, we have arranged to have racing, and the owners of these race-tracks have contributed hundreds of dollars. How did these 208
gentlemen come to be in a position to do so? Simply through the association realizing profits, and being on that account prosperous enough to help us. Farmers benefit therebv. The passing of this Bill would inflict heavy losses on those who interest themselves in the improvement of horsebreeding. What would be gained by ruining these men? What would become of these associations who contribute towards the improvement of agricultural methods, the desirability of which is acknowledged by all? Representatives of the people who are desirous of promoting the welfare and the development of the country should not hesitate a single moment to vote against this Bill.
The question has been asked whether or not such a measure would be easy of enforcement. I am now speaking as if the Bill was to pass, although I do not think it will be voted by the House; but, admitting that it will pass, will it be an easy matter to enforce its provision? I have had some _ experience in the matter, having practised law for the last thirty years. I have always been concerned with my professional duties, and was deemed worthy of being appointed Crown prosecutor in my district. For the last four years, I have been acting in that capacity. Numbers of cases of all kinds have been brought up in the meantime, and having that experience, which should count for something, I say without hesitation that it would be absurd to pass such a law, to make betting a criminal act, to deal with bettors as if they were scoundrels and criminals, and that you will fail in getting a jury to condemn people charged with such an offence. Jurymen as a rule are respectful of authority, but they are free and independent men, and called upon as they are to decide as to the fact independently of the law, they will be averse to returning a verdict against that man, large amounts will have been expended in vain, public morals, public interests, nobody in fact being benefited thereby. I say: no, that cannot be. You will not submit that citizen to such vexatious and useless annoyance. Besides, in doing so, you would not attain your object. Your charges would be met by denials and counter charges against the accuser. The putting in our statute-books of such an enactment far from giving security to citizens, would result merely in an expenditure of public funds to the injury of the accused.
Abuses have been alleged; instances have been cited of people who have spent extravagant amounts in betting, or of others who have in consequence committed thefts. That puts me in mind of scenes often witnessed at sittings of the criminal courts; and I may be allowed to recall them to the hon. member who made U3e

of that argument, at the same time that I appeal to the experience of those who know what is the general run of things at such sessions. Let us take the- case of a bankrupt. His liabilities aggregate a large amount; he is called upon to explain Low it is that, having a few months previously submitted a balance-sheet showing a rather large surplus, he is now confronted with such a deficit. That man is chary of telling the truth. He does not like the idea of admitting that he has obtained advances from his creditors under false pretenses. He deos not like to say that he was stock gambling, that his expenditure exceeded his revenue, that through speculations he lost money, that his wife has been spending the season at summer re-sorfs in the midst of great luxury, spending freely, or that he has made a trip to Europe when he had not the means of doing so. He will say: I lost money betting on horses. Why does he give such an excuse? Because he is well aware that nobody is in a position to verify his statement, or to find out with whom he engaged in betting. It is the same with those who conceal stolen goods: invariably, they say they have bought the goods from a fellow passing on the street, and whom they do not know. That is the answer always in stock. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, whenever a man has something to hide, some wrongdoing to conceal, some crime to cover up, his last resource is always to say: I have been gambling on the race-track. That is what makes me suspicious of the evidence taken before the committee. Of course, such an excuse may be accepted for once; but when a man says: I have been a regular gambler, I have lost my money betting on the race-track, I say such a man should not ask the government to protect him. His relatives should see to it that he leads a less extravagant life, should see to it that he be, if necessary, interdicted, or provided with a judiciary council.
The instances brought forward by my hon. friends are of an exceptional nature and have not been made the subject of any subject to any special inquiry. They are of such an extraordinary nature that we are warranted in doubting, I do not say the word of those hon. gentlemen, but the truth of the statements of those who represent themselves as victims of such misfortunes, incorrectly so, to my mind. That is the excuse of all those who have n.ot the courage to acknowledge in what way they lost their fortune, in what way they courted ruin and failuie.
That suggests another thought to me. How is it that the French laws which were kept in force at the time of the conquest, how is it that the civil code of the province of Quebec contain provisions permitting gambling and betting on the racetrack? Supposing that Bill amending the Mr. LAFORTUNE.
Criminal Code should come into force, I wonder which of the two would supersede the other? Would precedence be given in this connection to the Dominion law which prohibits such a deed under penalty and imprisonment? But that would not change the provision of the provincial law or of the civil code which allow racing and even grant the right of recovering before the law courts the amount of any deposit made in that connection. Here then we have a subject of His Majesty governed by a double set of laws, under two jurisdictions. Under the one, he may have to appear before the criminal court; under the other he has the right to institute a civil action. Under sections 227 and following of the Criminal Code, that man may be arraigned before the courts of criminal jurisdiction, and penalized in consequence, while under the law of our province, he may enter a lawsuit before the civil courts against the party failing to make good a bet. I do not think that is a very enviable position to be in. It is downright encroachment. That shows how dangerous it is to introduce measures of that kind, to declare applicable to the whole of Canada such provisions, because abuses have cropped up at Toronto or Vancouver. I am in a position to state that not a single case of that sort has been brought to the knowledge of the authorities in my province.
I have not time just now to give the names of the men who compose that fine association of the Montreal Jockey Club and the Delormier Park Association. I shall have an opportunity later on to refer once more' to that, and to acquaint the House with the men who are at the head of those great associations we are so proud of. But when I see an enactment of that kind on the point of being inserted in our statutes, I say it is time we should cry out to the promoters of such a Bill: Stop, you are on the wrong track, you are proposing a law which should not be passed. I hope the time is not far when the movers of such proposals, and their partisans, will find out that the majority is not disposed to subserve the ambitions and aims of a few men madlv desirous of reforming others, though it would be in order for them to start by reforming themselves.
The evidence taken before the committee has been referred to. Mention has been made of a most distinguished gentleman, possessed of wide experience. Extracts have been quoted from the evidence of Dr. McEachern, who formely lived in Montreal and who now resides in Chateauguay county. It -was a matter of surprise to me to hear the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Miller) state that Dr. McEachern approved of his Bill. The evidence show the contrary to be the truth. I state to the House, under my responsibility as one of its mem-

hers, that the evidence given by Dr. Mc-Eachern is in direct condemnation of this Bill. I have gone over all his statements with great care. Dr. McEachern is well known in Montreal. He is a typically honest, conscientious and able man, possessed with wide experience, sensible, distinguished and considered by all. Well, I take Dr. McEachern's own evidence, as being in direct condemnation of the proposal brought forward by my learned opponent. I say that there is enough in such evidence to bury out of sight the Bill now under discussion.
I regret, though not for the sake of the House who may think I have spoken at too great a length, but for the sake of my hon. friends, that I should have to cut short my remarks. However, let them not lose courage, as I have much more yet in store for them. I ask to be permitted to resume my seat until 1 am given another opportunity to speak again.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are now well into the sixth month since the session opened, and I am sure that every one is anxious to see it come to a close. The government have yet many important measures to deal with. The House has been occupied with this Bill for two days, and we are still considering the first clause. In these circumstances I shall try to be as brief as possible and, if I can, to go straight to what seems to me to be the point of the matter for consideration. We have had upon the statute-book now for eighteen years and more our present law, the salient feature of which in regard to this particular matter at any rate is that it excepts from the operation of the section with regard to book-making, bets made on the racecourse of an incorporated association during the actual progress of a race-meeting. I suppose we must take it that that law has been found by experience not to work satisfactorily because this House, I assume, has by passing the second reading of this Bill, and by carrying the. motion to resolve ourselves into Committee of the Whole, adopted the principle that our present law is unsatisfactory, and that some change ought to be made in it. The question then for consideration now is what change we ought to make, and by the motion which was made at the rising of the committee last night we have presented an alternative proposition to that which the special committee in this case has recommended. The feature of the work of the special committee, I take it, has been that they have struck out altogether in the; proposed legislation the clause which in the existing law protects bets made during a racemeeting upon the race-track of an incorporated association. Having done that advisedly, having done that because they thought 2081
that change ought to be made, they propose to further that effort by altering the definition of a common betting place which appears in the earlier clauses of the Bill. As against the Bill drawn in that way the alternative which is proposed by the amendment is that we adopt, with a modification, the present English law, and I must say at once, so far as I am concerned, looking at it I suppose from the standpoint of a lawyer, that to my mind there is no comparison between the language of the draughtsmen, and the method which is used in these two efforts to get at the same result. The English Bill might almost be called a model of skilful legislation. It was prepared, it is said, by the late Lord Davey, and mentioning his name is sufficient to everj lawyer to remind him of one of the greatest lawyers who ever practised, or who ever adorned the English bench. The object of that Bill is accomplished in the fewest possible words, and in clear and distinct language by which exactly what is aimed at is struck, and a result reached about which I venture to think there is no room for doubt. As between the work of preparation, and as between the practical working of the two Bills, if it were a question of either being in operation, I feel satisfied there is every element of superiority in the English Bill over the one which has been reported by the committee, and which I think I may without disparagement refer to as the Yankee Bill, because it assumes to have adopted the same means to reach the desired ends which have been adopted in some of the states of the American union. For that reason I certainly would prefer the amendment which has been proposed to the report of the subcommittee itself.
