There is just one other thing I ought to say in that regard. My hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) read yesterday a letter I had written to him some two months ago on this subject. I certainly have no objection to his putting the letter on the pages of ' Hansard ' although I ought to say I never expected to see it there, and thought'I was merely writing to him as one member of the House might wright to another what my ideas were with reference to this question. The language of the letter expresses in perhaps as concise form as I could use, my views about this matter. I do think it is an extraordinary way of getting at the desired object to resort to the criminal law and to make something a crime which the ordinary sense of the average man does not consider a crime. We are piling up day by day crimes, and under our constitution we are leaving it to somebody else, as we have to do, to enforce these laws which make new crimes, and make people liable to criminal prosecutions for doing things in connection with

which many of us think there is no harm in the world. I do not know where it is going to end. We have had during the short time I have been in this House a very stringent law which makes it a crime to fish or indulge in what many people regard as comparatively innocent amusement on Sunday. We have passed a law making it a crime for a boy, all but grown up, to smoke a cigarette. We are now proposing to pass a law which will make it a crime for a man to make a bet, it may be with a young friend of either sex. Very possibly before the end of this parliament, we shall have a proposition to make it a crime to play cards, or to dance, or to indulge in any of the other amusements which there are some in the community think constitute very nearly, if not quite a sin. I deprecate that manner of legislation, I am sorry it should be necessary, and with regard to the particular thing in hand, the regulating of a race-meeting, I pointed out ig the letter I have been referring to that the right way as it seemed to me to do that was by the conditions upon which a license might be issued. The liquor traffic is regulated under license of our various provincial legislatures, and is well regulated in practice, nobody complains, we know that the working out practically of the regulating system which is under the control of the provincial legislatures by virtue of their power to issue licenses is satisfactory in regard to the carrying on of even so delicate a kind of business as the traffic in intoxicatingjiquor. Is it not manifest that it would be equally easy, perhaps more easy, to regulate the way in which racing associations should carry on their meetings-what kind of betting they should allow or what kind they should prevent, how many days they should hold their meetings, and what intervals should require to elapse between each of two meetings, and every other condition connected with the racing which is sought to be struck at by this legislation- by resorting to the various provincial legislatures and obtaining me necessary legislation from those bodies? I am very sorry that course has not been thought to be the wise one by those right-minded people who want to do what they consider to be for the welfare of the community, and who, instead of taking that course, have been advised to seek to make a new crime, or to add to the list of crimes already on the statute-book, by the legislation now before this House. But the Bills are here, and the question is, what disposition ought to be made of them? For my part, notwithstanding the presence in the draft of the proposed amendment of the clause referred to, providing that if a race-meeting continues for not more than twelve days and after an interval of at least twenty days between each of two Mr. AYLESWORTH.
meetings, the saving clause of the last section of the Bill shall apply to it-notwithstanding the presence of that provision, which I think is to be regretted, I for my part so much prefer that way of reaching the evil which is sought to be prevented, that I intend to support the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from West Northumberland (Mr. McColl). The difference in principle between the two schemes of getting at the trouble is that the English Bill strikes at the person who does the thing which it is sought to prohibit. It provides that every person who does these particular things-frequents or loiters in streets or other public places' for the purpose of book-making or betting-is liable to punishment, The Canadian Bill, or the Yankee Bill, the Bill reported by the committee, proceeds on the contrary idea of striking at the place where the thing is done. It prohibits the keeping of a 'common betting place,' and defines the words 'common betting place' by language wide enough to include everything, even the perambulating of a book-maker about the grounds of a race-track; and the result of so widening that definition is that it exposes to the danger of a prosecution any person on the grand stand at a race-meeting who makes a bet with his neighbour of either sex. That is, I think, an objection to this Bill. Let me point out how that result is reached. In the first place, the protection of the existing law is struck out, so that you have the prohibition, not it may be of individual betting, but at all events of the recording, noting down even in a pocket diary or upon one's shirt cuff, of the fact that a bet has been made, the amount of it, or the odds. Any one who does that, if this Bill as reported by the committee is passed, is liable to a year's imprisonment. That is the distinct provision of section 235 as reported without the saving clause, which is struck out:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence, and liable to one year's imprisonment, and to a fine not exceeding $1,000 who records any bet or wager upon the result of any race.
Then, the language of this clause, with the saving protection which the existing law contains struck out, is quite wide enough to cover, and I fancy will some day or other be sought to be made to cover, things that are not meant to be covered at all. 'Any bet upon any contest or trial of skill of man or beast.' I wonder if the draftsman thought of the ordinary game of bridge among four men. I think that is a contest or "trial of skill, largely so; and it is not unusual, I am told by those who play, that there should .be money staked upon the result. Then, with regard to the individual bet-using that phrase as in-

tending to describe a bet made between two people who are sitting side by side in the grand stand looking at an ordinary horse-race-the definition of a common betting place is completely metamorphosed. Under the existing law, 'common betting house' was the expression used, and it was defined to be a 'house, office, room or other place.' The word 'place' is used, but is used in such a collocation of words that it derives significance from the preceding phraseology-it means other place of the same character-a house, office, room or other place opened, kept or used. That is the present law. The use of the three verbs, 'opened, kept or used,' indicates at once a continuous and permanent usingopening it, starting it, keeping it, continuing it, using it in that sense-not for half an hour once in a year, but from day to day, continuously, is the idea conveyed. All that has been carefully swept away, deliberately swept away by this Bill, because the proposed amendment as reported by this committee is a common' betting 'place,' not 'house' as at present-'a place,' not 'opened, kept and used,' but simply ' used ' for the purpose of betting between persons resorting thereto,' and second, 'any person using the same.' Then we have at the end of that section this sweeping definition of the word 'place,' which was intended, as I said on the second reading, to get rid of any idea of fixity in the word 'place,' and to make that word include the up-and-down course which any one might take in walking or strolling about a race-track:
The word 'place' as used in this section and in the preceding section, includes any place, whether inclosed or not, and whether it is used permanently or temporarily, and whether there is or is not exclusive right of user.
Now what have we to say about all this? I take the case of two young people sitting side by side in adjoining seats in the grand stand. "Clearly they are occupying a place within that definition. 'Place' is meant to include any place, whether inclosed or not, whether it is used permanently or temporarily. Although persons may be sitting there only half an hour, they are occupying a place within the meaning of this law. Whether they have or not the exclusive right of user, the very fact that they are there on that occasion makes this description clearly applicable to them. Is a person sitting there looking at the races, a person who is using that seat for the purpose of betting with his neighbour? I do not think it would be a far cry for a magistrate so to hold, and I apprehend in all seriousness that, if this measure should pass in the form in which it is reported by the special committee, any one who chooses to institute a prosecution against a visitor at the races for having made a bet of a pair of gloves with his fair companion, will have a perfectly plausible case to present. It may be said that such a thing will not happen. I only point out the distance to which this legislation is going when what many of us at least think harmless is being constituted a crime.

I have listened, Mr. Speaker, with great interest to the very learned discourse we have just heard from the Iron. Minister of Justice (Mr. Ayles-worth) and I only regret that my duties in committee have kept me away to-day and prevented my listening to all the discussion on the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. McColl). The hon. the Minister of Justice has brought his great mind to bear on this, and I think has very successfully pointed out all the weak spots of the Bill, but very steadily avoided the main point at issue. I do not want to charge the hon. minister with not treating the committee fairly. It is only due to him to say that, in all probability, he did not know that the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Miller) said yesterday, and has said time and time again, that when this Bill reached the committee stage he intended to move an amendment which would enable two friends sitting at the grand stand in a race meet to bet on the result, if they wanted to do ;o. But the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) and those supporting the amendment would bowl this Bill out because they say it contains that stipulation. I admit that it does and that such a provision is not proper legislation, but I want to see the Bill get before the committee and be discussed clause by clause; and when we come to any clause not in the interests of the public, I reserve my right to vote against it.
We might as well state the issue and that is that the great difference between the Bill as reported by the Special Committee and the amendment of the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. McColl) is that in the one case we are trying to keep the book-maker off the racetrack and in the other we are leaving the door wide open. I propose to vote for the original Bill subject to the right to amend it when necessary, and I vote for it simply because I am opposed to book-making on the track. The Minister of Justice will not attempt to deny that, notwithstanding the beautiful language in which this proposed amendment is clothed, notwithstanding it may have been drafted by one of the greatest legal minds in England, notwithstanding its beautiful phraseology, it allows book-making to be carried on with impunity at any race meet practically in the Dominion. I am not

going into a long dissertation to show why I am onposed to book-making on the racetrack. I have never had the privilege of attending the meets at Toronto, Hamilton or Montreal, but I have attended races in my own province since I was a boy, and I am as much a lover of a good horse as even the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) or the hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth), and I make the statement that there has been hardly an honest race in the maritime provinces, the last five or ten years. I am not talking now simply for the purpose of hearing my own voice, but I know what I am talking about, I know there are proprietors of racetracks who have honestly tried to prevent these dishonest transactions, but so long as the book-maker is allowed to go on the track and carry on his business, so long will you have dishonest horse-racing. In the maritime provinces, as a rule, the races are sold before they are competed, and the innocent man who bets is simply betting with the dice loaded against him every time.
I am not going to discuss whether we can have horse-breeding without racing. I can only say that twenty years ago when we did not have any of these nefarious practices in the maritime provinces, we bred just as good horses as we are doing to-day. If you go down to the maritime provinces and ask any one who is in the habit of going to the races whether he is going now, he will say, no, that the races are sold out in advance. If you can eliminate bookmaking, you will have honest racing. The opponents of this Bill have done all they possibly could to defeat it. I thought that the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. McColl) had made a very fair argument yesterday afternoon, but the substance of it was that if you do not allow betting you cannot have horse-racing. I take issue with my hon. friend. The next argument was that these running horses or thoroughbreds are necessary in the interests of horse-breeding. I take issue with that statement. If you had all the running horses and thoroughbreds in the country, they would hardly run one good farm or lumber camp. If rich people want to purchase such horses, that is their own affair, but such horses are not the class which form the back-bone and wealth of this country. I do not think that 99 out of 100 of our horses would suffer very much if this class were not encouraged. But I do not admit that you cannot encourage it without betting. The only question is * whether or not book-making shall be allowed on the race-track, and being convinced that it should not, and that public sentiment is opposed to it, I shall vote in favour of the Bill.

I quite agree with a good deal that has been said by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth), but there is one thing he said with which I do not agree, and that is that, in voting for the second reading, we committed ourselves to an attack on the race-tracks. What I understand is that all we committed ourselves to is the necessity of amending the law in some way so as to prohibit the vice of gambling in toto, so far as we can assume that it is a vice. Now, the question before the committee has narrowed down to this: Which is the best means to restrain the vice of gambling, if it be a vice? I do not say it is a vice; I never gambled myself, but I think a man has a right to gamble if his conscience tells him there is no harm in it. But, while that is my personal attitude, my opinion on the public question is that you cannot build up the manhood of this country by shackling the individual citizen so that it is impossible for him to do anything but what some particular person may think is in full accord with the beau ideal of righteousness. If you wish to build up the manhood of Canada, particularly among the young, you must teach them to resist temptation. You must so conduct public affairs as to appeal to their manhood, and you must teach them that only as they resist temptation will they grow in moral strength. Now, I am interested in voting for what my constituency thinks is best for the moral interest of the country. I have had a lot of petitions sent to me, not exactly praying, but almost commanding me, to vote for the Bill of the hon. gentleman for South Grey (Mr. Miller) in its entirety. I have had sensible' letters and petitions sent from other people asking me to do the opposite in the interest of the horse-breeding industry. Now, what am I to do? I say that my duty is to do what is best to prohibit as much as possible the vice of gambling, if it be a vice. What would this Bill do? It would make illegal every form of gambling in which one has to deal with a professional. But, if you adopt the amendment of the hon. member for West Northumberland (Mr. McColl) you permit this kind of betting to be carried on in certain places where it is natural for it to be carried on, but you prohibit it in other places. You have, as it were, a vent-you allow the man who wants to make a bet to make it legally under conditions that are natural. For my part, if I had time, I would go to all the races, and I think I should never want to make a bet at all. But if a man does want to make a bet, is it not better that there should be a place where he can do it without being branded as a criminal? If you tell the people that they must not make a bet anywhere, betting will be carried on in a hypocritical way, these professionals will pretend to be private bettors, the ag-

gregate amount of betting will be more, and it will be done in defiance of the law, which is far worse for public morals than the condition which it is sought here to remedy. 1 believe sincerely that under the amendment of the hon. member for West Northumberland there will be less gambling in the aggregate and also less hypocrisy in regard to it. And the development of this hypocrisy is much worse than to leave a man uninterfered with who, as the. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) said, may wish to make a private bet, for instance, at the St. Catharines regatta, or at a football match. My hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller), in my opinion- perhaps he does not care about that-is making a tactical mistake in the course he pursues in regard to this Bill. I made a suggestion to him yesterday with regard to the reading of the evidence which had only been printed in English. But, though he may not care for my opinion on the matter, I give him that nevertheless. If he is sincere, as I admit he is, I think he would have done better to have accepted the amendment of the hon. member for West Northumberland. I believe that under that amendment the country will make more progress in restraining the evil of gambling, if it be an evil, than would be made under the law which the hon. member (Mr. Miller) proposes. One great advantage would be that the House would then be unanimous, and the House being unanimous, the country, public opinion, would be behind it. The disadvantage is that, if we are not united in a matter of this kind, the people tend to take sides. Where public opinion is not strongly behind such a law as this, it cannot be well enforced, and the evasion of the law creates a class of hypocrites. I am bound to say that in the interest of morality, according to my judgment, the amendment of the hon. member for West Northumberland is the best legislation for us to pass.
Now, let me say a word about the horsebreeding industry. The gentlemen who tell me that this Bill will interfere with thf horse-breeding industry are not the rich men pictured by the hon. member foi Carleton, New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell) but they include in their numbers the stalwart fruit-growers of the county of Lincoln, who must have horses with a certain speed in their composition. I do not agree with the view expressed by some hon. members that the automobile is going to put the horse out of business. I think that the horse is still the noble animal and man's true friend that we were taught in school t,o believe him to be, and that he has great usefulness still. The fruit-growers of Niagara district need fast-going horses. They need horses with some strength, but they need speed also. Their product, fruit, is a perishable commodity, and it must be sent
out fresh, and to be sure of catching the train which is to carry that fruit to market, horses with some speed are absolutely necessary. That is one reason why I think it is not quite fair to say that this legislation would interfere only with rich people who own running horses or fast trotting horses. For the reasons I have given, 1 feel bound to vote for the amendment of the hon. member for West Northumberland.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that I should have a few words to say in regard to this Bill before the vote is taken, more particularly by reason of the fact that one of the racing-tracks spoken of, and spoken of in a somewhat derogatory manner is owned-or rather, hot owned, but operated-in the constituency which I, for the time, have the honour to represent. The learned counsel who looked after the interests of the promoters of this Bill saw fit to place the Fort Erie track and the Windsor track in a class by themselves. and, in his estimation, rather below the standard of such tracks as the Woodbine at Toronto, the track at Hamilton, and the track at Montreal. I presume that he made these statements because he was not aware of the facts as they exist. But I can tell him, as I tell this House, that there is no racing-track in Canada that is up to the standard, as a racing-track, of the track at Fort Erie. It is the best track by far that there is in this Dominion. And it is conducted now, and has been conducted from its inception, in as high and straightforward and honest a way as any racetrack in Canada. It is true that the tracks at Fort Erie and Windsor have had racing days extending over a longer period than other tracks. But why? One reason is that they do not get the same numbers of people as does the track meet in Toronto. Toronto is a large city, and the racing meet is a great social event; all society turn out to attend that meeting, wearing their best clothes and looking very gay and/ happy and comfortable. The association has iarge gate receipts and can afford to pay large purses with a shorter number of days' racing than Fort Erie. In order to get the same class of horses at the Fort Erie and Windsor tracks as they have in Toronto it is necessary, from a financial point of view, to have a longer racing-meet than would be necessary in Toronto or Montreal. But I say, and any one who has visited these tracks, particularly any one who has visited the Fort Erie track during the racing-meet, will unite with me in ..saying, that the racing-meetings at Fort Erie are conducted on as high a plane as those of any of the other tracks in Canada. So. I wish, on behalf of the people of the county of Welland, to repudiate the suggestion that has gone forth that there is any violation of the moral law taking place on the

Fort Erie track other than on anv other track.
Now I was rather pleased to hear the speech of the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Stratton) on this question. He made such a speech as he usually makes in discussing public questions, and with^ a large portion of his speech I agree. For instance, he said it made no difference to him by whom this Bill was promoted, whether by the Lord's Day Alliance or by any other combination of people, and with that I agree. I know that the Lord's Day Alliance so-called, in the province of Ontario at any rate, has done a very large amount of good in maintaining the moral standard of the people of that province. I am quite willing to concede that, and I trust and believe that they will continue to do good. But when they, or when any other person says to me, or to other people in the province of Ontario, that what we have been in the habit of doing, what we have been brought up to believe is not a crime, is a crime, and that we are criminals in doing those things, then I object to that proposition. I do not think that they have a right to curtail freedom of action in those particulars. There is in this country a very wide divergence of opinion as to what can he done within the bounds of moral rectitude, and honour. A large number of people claim that running street cars on Sunday is a crime, that running electric cars through the country on that day is a crime. We know that some years ago when the Toronto Street Car Company desired to get a Bill passed to allow them to operate street cars on Sunday, they met with an enormously strong opposition. Many times that Bill went before the electors, and many times it was defeated, until eventually it was carried. Well, Sir, the street cars have been running in Toronto since then against the -wishes of a large class of people. But I would like to ask any hon. gentleman in this House to-day what they think would be the result if a by-law was submitted to the people of Toronto now to stop the running of street cars on Sunday? Does not any person feel that such a bylaw would be overwhelmingly defeated? The street cars are running to the benefit of the people of the city of Toronto. So it is with regard to many other things, with regard to these finer- moral questions. I can also agree with the statement of the Minister of Justice that we are putting on the statute-book of Canada legislafion declaring matters to be crimes- which the general consensus of opinion throughout the country feel are not crimes at all.
Now there is a considerable degree of misunderstanding in regard to matters pertaining to the race-track. I have heard the book-makers condemned here very severely.
I have no love for the book-makers, I am

not a defender of the book-makers, I do not care anything about book-makers, whether they are on the track or not. But what I say is that we should not by legislation declare to be a crime what is a simple bet between individuals on the track, and that is what this law does, and if this legislation is adopted, that will be the result of it. The law in Canada in regard to this matter stood in one particular way for a great many years. But in 1892 it was thought that the law did not go far enough in exempting betting on race-tracks, and Sir John Thompson, who was then Minister of Justice, in consolidating the Criminal Code of Canada, introduced into the Bill a further exception. In section 235 of the Act, after the words ' to bets between individuals,' these words were added:
Or made on the race-course of an incorporated association during the actual progress of a race-meeting.
At that time the matter was discussed very fully. Sir Louis Davies, who is now one of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada, in speaking upon that matter said that parliament should thoroughly understand what they were doing, that they were legalizing bets that were made on the racetrack. That was thoroughly discussed, and understood, and parliament at that time unanimously decided that that should be done, and the law has stood that way ever since. For myself I cannot see that any harm has been done by reason of that enactment, and that is the way that I for one would like to see it stand in the future. I think that this, parliament, in eliminating that exception to the clause 235, is going further than it should go in this direction. There is another section of the Bill which it seems to me is not- at all in the interest of the public, and that is in prohibiting the publishing of racing news. What, would be the result? You would prevent Canadian newspapers from publishing the iftws, whereas the United States papers*, which publish the same news, are delivered in Toronto in the morning almost as early as the Toronto papers, and you would cut off a considerable source of revenue to the Canadian newspapers. People who desired to procure this news would get United States papers instead. It seems to me that this Bill is one that should not pass, at any rate in its present form. The Bill which is introduced as an amendment is one which it seems to me will answer every purpose that is required, and to that I shall give my approval.

I feel great pleasure at being in accord with many of my hop. friends opposite in regard to this measure,
] and particularly I am so pleased to be in accord with the hon. member for Carleton,
I New Brunswick, (Mr. Carvell), that I must

indulge myself in making a few remarks. The hon. member for Carleton has come closer to my way of thinking, and his process of reasoning is more in accord with my own, than that of any other speaker who has addressed the House. In all matters of this character, matters that involve moral questions requiring legislation, we are led to conclusions through instinct, and an impulse of the heart, rather than by a distinct movement of the mind. Having taken up our position, which the great body of the public have taken with us, me circulation of information, and the advance of thought bringing each ultimately -to the same conclusion, we look back, and try to find some process of reasoning, some pathway of thought by which we have arrived at that conclusion. There are two elements connected with the question, the hon. member for Regina (Mr. W.^M. Martin), yesterday stated one of them,* and he conceived it to be all. He stated that all each member of this House had to decide in his own mind was whether or not the institution of betting was a right or a wrong institution. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) took him to task for that statement, and I think rightly, but the hon. member for Brandon substituted in its place the proposition that all this House had to decide was whether it was for the good, the peace, and welfare of society to pass this Bill, or whether it was not, and that in coming to that conclusion the individual opinion of any hon. member of this House, as to the rightness or wrongness of betting, had nothing whatever to do with the case. With the latter statement made by the hon. member for Brandon I disagree just as firmly as I disagree with the statement of the hon. member for Regina. I believe with him that each member of this House, before he can intelligently defend his vote on this question, must decide whether the practice and institution of betting are right or wrong, and whether they are for the public good, the public weal or the public ill, as now conducted. I cannoit conceive of any hon. member of this House voting to place in the category of crimes a practice which he in his heart believes to be good, and right, and in the interests of society. I believe that before he can vote for the Miller Bill he must, as one of the incidents of such decision, decide affirmatively that the practice of betting per se, is wrong as at present conducted. But I feel that he has more than that to decide. I do not think he has proceeded sufficiently far when he determines that in his view it would be better if this institution could be suppressed. He must also persuade himself that the general sentiment of the country, the sentiment of the people for whom he is legislating, is not only numerically in its favour, but is numerically sufficiently
strong, and sufficiently impelling to enable the law to be enforced reasonably once it is placed upon the statute-book. Whether I agree with any other hon. member or not, my line of thought brings me to the conclusion that once an hon. member is convinced that the practice of betting does no good, but does harm, once he is convinced that the putting down of the practice, or a branch of the practice, a branch of the tree or the institution, if you cannot do it. all, will be sufficiently supported by the public to ensure its reasonable enforcement, he must support the Bill and I cannot see how he can defend on the platform a vote against it. Those who agitate for the amendment do not contend, and I do not believe they can contend, that the amendment aims at or pretends to effect any further advance in the suppression of betting than does the Bill itself. The only difference between the amendment, and the Bill, that is in so far as the principle is concerned, leaving aside the details, and the expressions which may be adjusted in committee, is that the amendment leaves out unscathed, and untouched the practice of betting on race-tracks. That is to say that just as soon as the institution of betting stands out exposed, clear, in the light of the public eye, just as soon as we get on. the fashionable race-track, we leave it untouched, we license it, and we declare it to be right. The question of where the amendment will lead is reduced down to one naked principle, and one alone. Whether or not a practice, which, if it is wrong per se, must be suppressed, can be right when it reaches its highest state of evolution, is exposed to the public view, and caters to the young and weak. To my mind' the effort of those who will not support the Bill, and who. dare not oppose it, is to effect their purpose not by denying the passage of the Bill, but by frittering it away by amendments.
I 'stated when I started out that there were two elements to the question under discussion-first of all the rightness or wrongness of the institution of betting, and, secondly, the question of public opinion. For my part I take the ground that the institution of betting in itself has done nobody any .good in this world. I do not believe that under its best conditions it ever does any good, and-I believe it does infinite harm. The institution of betting; when you wipe away the verbiage, when you look down at the prin-eiple of its being, its heart, and life, what is it? It is the attempt to get in this world by chance what should be got only by industry and toil. It is really based upon the desire to get the wages of this life without. working for them. It is an effort to get the rewards of doing well by doing ill, an effort to get the prizes of life by doing in



jury to one's fellows instead of doing them good. I am quite aware that for generations, and generations unknown during the past men have indulged in that practice, but I believe that what in one age may be a pleasureable habit may, in the next age, be a crime. This word ' crime ' has been taken in this debate to mean something much more vicious than it logically should mean in a discussion of this sort? What is a crime? A crime may not be anything so very hideous. A crime is something which, for the purpose and good of society, is condemned as not in the interest of society, whereas, once, perhaps, it was not against the interests of society. It is something that the consensus of public opinion has affirmed that it is better to do without than to do with, though it might perhaps in certain cases do good concomitant with it. What was not a crime in the last century may be a crime in this. What is not a crime in Russia may be a crime in Canada. What was certainly not a crime in the days of Pitt may be a crime to-day. While I may never-have made a bet in my life, may never even have been tempted in the matter, because, aside altogether from the moral considerations, during a large part of my life I had a very good reason for not betting, I am aware that the brightest mind that ever adorned the mother of parliaments was the most profligate bettor in the whole of the motherland. I am aware that the best men or some of the best of men of all ages, have indulged in betting, and I believe they did so conscientiously; and possibly under the conditions of society then existing they were doing no wrong, and it would not have been in the interests of that society to endeavour to suppress betting. But I believe that day has gone by. I believe that betting as they have it to-day has done harm, and great harm. I appeal to the judges quoted by the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mir. Maddin), and to the other authorities quoted by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. W. M. Martin), I appeal to the unanimous verdict of bench and pulpit, and to other institutions just as venerable throughout Great Britain, and throughout Greater Britain, and I appeal to my own experience and to my own observations throughout the years I have been able to observe, and I for one am convinced that if this parliament had it in its power to suppress utterly the whole institution of betting they would be doing a good service to society.
I do not follow the argument of hon. gentlemen who affirm that so long as we leave out betting in this form or in that form, we acknowledge the principle of betting to be good. I leave out betting in certain forms, I leave out betting in private houses and in some other places, not because it is not wrong in itself and should Mr. MEIGHEN.
not be suppressed, but because it is beyond the power of parliament and beyond the power of the law to suppress it. and because public opinion is not sufficiently far advanced to warrant such legislation and to ensure its enforcement. When I find the element of gambling removed from the business element and clearly disclosed in its naked deformity, I say it is the duty of parliament to strike at it as soon as we find we effectively can. My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) pointed out that the element of betting entered into the practice of life insurance. He is quite right. Another gentleman said that the element of chance entered into transactions in groceries and in stocks. They are right too. But where chance enters into these transactions, it is not the only element, in some it is a very minor element, and it is impossible to eliminate that element of chance in betting and leave the rest. It is monstrous to think we can do so at present. Just as soon as we can I am prepared to legislate against the element of chance in these respects as well as in the form in which we are now attacking it, that is the form of race-track gambling. In that form there is absolutely no other element except the element of gambling, it is gambling pure and simple. With the construction of mind with which I am afflicted I cannot follow the reasoning by which the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. McColl) arrives at the proposition that a man might gamble and still not be a gambler. It would be as reasonable to say that a man might murder and still not be a murderer. He might not be a professional gambler, but he could not gamble without gambling any more than he could murder without murdering. I do not wish to place the two in the same category. 1 believe that betting in many ways is but a slight offence and that in many cases it may do no harm, but it never does any good, and as an institution it brings about infinite misery and pain.
Is the public opinion of this country sufficiently strong to warrant this parliament in passing legislation in its present form? There may be a difference of opinion in that regard, there may be hon. members who are in a better position to judge of that than I. The hon. member for Brandon affirms that it is not, and he bases his affirmation on the statement that there was no discussion of this subject at the last election, and on the further statement that no public meetings have been called to demand this legislation, and that there has been no unanimity of opinion among the press of this country. If those three considerations exist and he is right in regard to them he would repeal almost half the whole Criminal Code. In the first place as regards discussion at the last election, every one knows that we were so busy discussing the

hon. member for Brandon and much of his history that we had not much time to discuss gambling and other subjects. But how much of the Criminal Code, what single act or habit which has been denied to humanity by our whole code has been asked for at a general election? What single provision has received the unanimous endorsation of the press? What single provision was passed by parliament by reason of public meetings throughout Canada demanding its passage? To every one of these questions the hon. member for Brandon would have to say, none. He says we have no indication that public opinion is behind this Bill. I ask him what significance attaches to the fact that for months our desks each morning have been covered with petitions like a snowstorm? Has any legislation ever been proposed to us for consideration that has been so thoroughly, so emphatically demanded by the people of Canada as this Bill? I do not know of any,
I have not heard of any, I have not heard that since confederation a single principle -of legislation or a single Bill was ever demanded in the form of petitions as unanimously as this Bill. I look to that, but I look further. I must admit in candour that doubtless a great many signed these petitions without any real appreciation of the legislation for which they were asking. I believe that applies to all petitions. I look to my own constituency, which adjoins Brandon; I believe that in my constituency as in that of the hon. member for Brandon there are a great many good people, better than I am and perhaps better than he is, who are opposed and conscientiously opposed to that legislation. But I believe the great mass of the people in both constituencies demand it, and judging other constituencies by these I conclude that there is a general demand for this legislation. These constituencies are no better and no worse than the average constituency in this country. They are constituencies that may well be taken as examples. There are cities in both, there are race-tracks in both, there are jockey clubs or similar institutions in both; those institutions are at one in demanding the negativing of this Bill, and the remainder of the people demand its passing. Consequently I think that if they may be taken as examples, and I think they should, they will illustrate that the great mass of public sentiment to an extent quite up to that pointed out by the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Stratton) is in favour of this legislation. I do not think the hon member for Peterborough at all overstated the case. I believe that if a vote were taken in Manitoba, just as he said if it were taken in Ontario, 80 per cent of the voters would vote in favour of the suppression of race-track gambling. I do not think these figures overstate the fact. It is quite true that there may be constituencies more directly interested which are not of the same complexion; but, taking it all in all, I am of opinion that the public sentiment of this country demands this legislation, and that to deny it would be not to bring the law into contempt, as the hon. member for Brandon suggested, but rather to bring down in the estimation of the people of this country the standard of the parliament of Canada. For these reasons, and for no other-because I arrive at my conclusion by a very simple process-I shall support the Bill, and I hope it will not be whittled away by the passage of this amendment or by any other that may be suggested.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I feel it necessary to call the attention of the committee to a point which probably should have been brought to their notice before. Had I been in the Chair last night when the amendment was offered, I would probably have called attention to it. The argument has turned so much on the proposed amendment that perhaps it has been delayed too long. The rule in discussing Bills in committee is that they shall be taken up clause by clause. This Bill has been announced, and clause No. 1 has been taken up. On this point Bourinot says of a Bill that has reached the committee:
It is then considered clause iby clause. Each clause is a distinct question, and must be separately discussed.
Rule 53 of the rules of the House says:
In proceedings in Committee of the Whole House upon Bills, the preamble is first postponed, and then every clause considered by the committee in its proper order.
The amendment offered to clause 1 is not strictly an amendment to clause 1; it proposes to introduce a new Bill entirely instead of the Bill before the House. It cannot be accepted as a proper amendment. There is nothing, however, to prevent the hon. gentleman presenting his views, clause by clause, or in any way that he desires; but, unless the committee should otherwise decide, I cannot consider this an amendment to clause 1.

I understand, then, from your ruling that the proper procedure would be this, that a vote should be taken on each clause of the Bill, and if the various clauses were defeated, then it would be proper for the hon. gentleman presenting this amendment to move each clause of it, so that it would became part of the Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. leader of the opposition has expressed my view of the matter.

den termination of the debate when the Speaker was in the Chair, some complaint having been made of that, I believe the general consensus of opinion expressed in the House was that those who desired to speak should be allowed to speak generally on the Bill, though in Committee of the Whole. On that understanding the debate has continued since, and, therefore, 1 would not regard it as being out of order. It was practically with the unanimous consent of the House, because as far as I heard, no one objected.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am not objecting to the debate. I am quite prepared to allow all the latitude which hon. members desire in discussing the Bill; but 1 feel that I cannot accept the amendment as an amendment to clause 1.
Notwithstanding that it is the understanding of the House that the question can be speedily settled in that way?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would not desire to place myself in antagonism to the unanimous view of the committee; yet the committee is bound by the rules of the House. The House itself can change its rules;,the committee cannot.
Do I understand, then, that this amendment may be moved w'hen the preamble is moved?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would think not, unless the committee chose to reconsider what it had already decided; because when the preamble is being considered, this amendment would very likely be a motion to change what the committee had already decided upon.
Then, according to your statement, you have no amendment before you at the present moment which can be moved' to any of the clauses of the Bill?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Do I undersand that a portion of this amendment may be moved as an amendment to the first clause?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Any amendment may be made to section 1 that is relevant to the subject it bears upon.

I think the situation is very clear under the ruling of the chairman. We are now dealing with the proposal to amend section 226 of the Criminal Code, and it is auite open to any hon. member of this House to propose Mr. SPROULE.
an amendment to section 226 of the Criminal Code in any other terms that he may see fit, or to move that section 1 be struck out altogether. But the chairman has ruled that we must take each section of the Bill in its turn, and if all the clauses of the Bill should be disposed of without all the amendments having been dealt with, then it would be proper to add to the Bill any clauses of the proposed amendment upon proper motion to that effect,
I understand that the Bill may be discussed, but not the amendment?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Clause 1 is before the committee, and it is the only clause that is before the committee; but. as the discussion has been very broad, I would not at all wish to confine it to that clause if it is the desire of the committee to discuss the principle generally.

Then I wish to say a few words with regard to the question. I would not possibly have said a word on the Bill now before the House had it not been for the fact that brought my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) to his feet. He wished to endorse the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell). It is because of a broad statement made by the hon. member for Carleton that I feel compelled to take part in this discussion. That hon. gentleman stated that not a race was started in the maritime provinces that was not sold before it started.
Mr, CARVELL. My hon. friend is not quoting me quite correctly, I stated that a very large proportion of those races were sold out before they started, and I repeat it.

I accept that, but I took the words down as I stated them. I understand my hon. friend to say now that the greater proportion of the races which take place in the maritime provinces are sold out before they start.
I stand by that statement.

Then my hon. friend will have very little to stand on by the time I have made my statement. In the principal province of the maritime provinces we have in the city of Halifax a track second to none, and perhaps the best track east of Montreal. We hold speed contests on that track once a year and for eight or ten days. That track is governed and controlled by an exhibition commission, which is appointed by the provincial government, the city council of Halifax, and the Farmers' Association of Nova Scotia. The best men go there and

no better men can be got anywhere. They control the race-track, they have had that race-track in operation some ten or twelve years, and I never heard any charge that any race at any of these meets was sold. We have no book-makers there and * no gambling. I have been at these races frequently, and have known many very prominent men from New Brunswick to bring their horses there.
And get fleeced too.

My hon. friend cannot produce any proof of that statement, but from what he has said they get fleeced in their own province. We have no such practices going on in our province as he refers to at the race meets in his. Let me say that the track at Halifax is one of the best, if not the best east of Montreal, and that what we give there is speed contests for which purses are offered. These contests are run under a board of management which would not permit any wrongdoing. If my hon. friend has any evidence in support of the statement he made about the race-track at Halifax, he ought to produce it or else retract what he said.
Being a layman I am not competent to give an opinion on the practical effect of this measure, but judging by the argument of the hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth), I am of the opinion that there is something in this measure I should not vote for, and that the amendment is one which I can fairly and honestly support. I only rose for the purpose of drawing attention to the statement of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) who has made a most unwarranted charge against prominent men of Halifax, and whose charge is contradicted by the very fact that leading horse-owners in New Brunswick patronize the race track in that city.

I did not intend to enter into a discussion with the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby) regarding what takes place in that noble city. I take full responsibility for every word I have said,
. and, notwithstanding the statement made by my hon. friend, I do not propose to withdraw a syllable. I did not say, anything about Halifax, but the trouble with this hon. gentleman is that he has a craze over Halifax, and thinks that Halifax is the only place on earth. It is quite a nice little place, but you cannot bring a subject up from the Lord's Day Bill down to the gambling transaction, but the city of Halifax must be brought into it. The best evidence that there is truth in what I have said will be found in the fact that it is not the people of Halifax or New Brunswick who are to blame, but the Americans who come over there in numbers with their horses and book-makers. It is they who make all the trouble. So great is
the evil that the Maritime Association ha3 passed within the last three weeks a resolution entirely excluding American horses except those coming from the northern part of Maine.

It is not my intention to detain the House very long. I do not wish that the few remarks I am about to make shall be construed as implying that I am opposed to any one owning a good race-horse, or attending a race-meet. The only thing I cannot understand is what connection there is between a race-track and gambling and betting. I have heard a good many arguments on both sides upon this Bill, but I have not heard any.,.good reason why I should not vote for it. There has not been a single argument brought forward which could induce me to vote for gambling on the race-track. As I understand this Bill, it is good legislation in the best interests of the people at large. The only great point which I think has been missed in the argument so far, is the influence which has been brought to bear upon the members of this House to vote for the Bill. When the Navy Bill was before us, many hon. members thought it would be a good idea to take the opinion of the people upon it before enacting any legislation. I would like to ask if there was ever a Bill introduced into this House in favour of which more petitions were presented than the one under discussion. Those petitions were scattered throughout' this Dominion. They were not circulated secretly; and if a large number of people are opposed to the measure, as some hon. members would lead us to believe, why have they not sent in petitions against it? I am not aware that a single petition has been presented in opposition to it. I would like to know if those who are opposed to this Bill would make that a plank in their platform at the next general election. Judging from the number of petitions presented, one would be led to believe that any one who would dare to vote in opposition to this Bill would be elected to stay at home.
I am not afraid to go back, and would like to fight the issue out with you.

We would see what the result would be. Hon. gentlemen opposite would lead you to believe that the Bill was opposed to the race-track. I do not understand it so. As I understand the Bill, it is opposed to the pernicious gambling that takes place on the race-track. It was argued by some hon. members that race-meet-inss could not be maintained without betting or gambling. I am informed by one of the hon. members for Prince Edward Island that they have good race-meetings there without betting. And the hon. mem-

her for Halifax (Mr. Crosby) has just told us that they have the best race-meetings, attended by the best class of people in this Dominion-most successful meetings-and no betting. And what was the testimony of the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin)? That hon. gentleman told us yesterday of ten places in Nova Scotia where they hold successful race-meetings without betting. Let me quote a few words from the hon. member from South Cape Breton as to how race-meetings are conducted there without gambling:
The horse-racing of Nova Scotia is as well conducted as that in any part of Canada, and it is carried on there without the assistance of book-makers or anything of that kind. The gentlemen who conduct the races in Nova Scotia are the equals of those who conduct horse-racing in any other part of Canada.
Now, I would ask the House: If you can have race-meetings in these different places successfully carried on without betting, why cannot we have them in Ontario and Quebec?
Again, we are told that we have no right to legislate for what is considered in the best interest of this country. I would like to know what the Department of the Minister of Justice exists for if it is not to legislate in the best interest of the people? The good book tells us: Thou shalt not steal. And we do not hesitate to legislate against stealing. Has not the parliament always legislated against evil? And, if that is the case, why should we not legislate against gambling at race-track meetings? I have here a document which was received, I think, by every member of this House, and perhaps by every member of the Senate. It reads as follows:

Methods used to influence members in its behalf.
The following is a copy of a letter sent broadcast throughout Canada to the clergy by S. D. Chown, general secretary of the Methodist Temperance and Moral Reform Department, and was published in the Toronto 'World' of March 28, showing the means used to influence the members of the Senate and House of Commons in securing their vote for the Miller Bill. The appeal is addressed to the dear brother, and reads as follows:
It would be of the highest importance if you would preach upon the subject of gambling on Sunday, April 3, or as soon thereafter as possible. If we have not already done so, we will supply you with material, immediately upon reuuest, which will be of assistance to you in the preparation of a suitable sermon. We have reached the crucial stage and must strain every nerve to succeed. If you could induce any of your influential men wisely to approach your representative in the House of Commons and any senators they may know-, in the interests of the Miller Bill, it would be well done just now.

This has been the system employed by this organization to secure the abolition of racing.
What do you think of it?
Now, I happen to know the gentleman referred to in this paper, Rev. Dr. Chown, and I want to say right here that there is not a clergyman in the Dominion of Canada who is held in higher esteem by the denomination to which he belongs than is Rev. Dr. Chown. It is for that reason that he was elected by the church to which he belongs to travel over this whole Dominion in the interest of temperance and moral reform. I am personally well acquainted with him, and I have never known him to issue a statement, in the press or otherwise, that he was ashamed to put his name to. But whoever issued the document I have just quoted was ashamed to put his name to it, and he winds up by asking: ' What do you think of it? ' I would ask any hon. member to point out a sentence in the address issued by Dr. Chown to his clergymen to which objection could be taken, coming from one in his position. And when this document winds up by asking: ' What do you think of it? ' 1 can only say that, so far as I 'am concerned, if race-tracks can only be maintained by betting and gambling, then, in the best interest of the -people of Canada, let the race-track go.

Just a very few words in connection with this Bill. So far as the promoters of the Bill are concerned, I am not inclined to agree in the animadversions passed upon these gentlemen, for I have no doubt that they have the best interest of the country at heart. Whatever may be said as to the advisability of some of the arguments put forward, I entirely agree that these gentlemen are engaged in endeavouring to deal with what is an admitted evil, and one which requires some legislative remedy. The debate, so far, has been upon the Bill as a whole. I do not want to deal at this moment with the Bill as a whole, nor with the amendment as a whole. I will speak of that a little later. There are some provisions in the Bill which I think are extreme. There are some considerations with respect to the amendment which lead me to believe, that, as it stands, it is not wholly satisfactory.
But first I wish to point out the remarkable situation with which parliament is confronted at the present time. The government of any country enjoying British institutions is supposed to deal with all legislation of an important character coming before parliament. The control of that legislation is with the government, and modern constitutional authorities, as well as those of not so recent date, impose upon the government the responsibility of dealing with matters of this character. I do not know of anv subject in respect

of which a greater responsibility is imposed upon the government of this or any other country than the control of criminal legislation. Surely, if there is one subject more than another as to which a government should be disposed to accept responsibilty, it is the framing and moulding and amendment of the criminal law. This Bill is legislation which the government of Canada considers of such great importance that it interrupts the government business for two days, and *calls upon parliament to deal with it. And we have the extraordinary spectacle of the Minister of Justice standing up in his place and saying that this Bill, for which the Tegular business of the country has been delayed, is not only of an extraordinary, but absolutely of an outrageous character.
I do not think any parallel to this situation can be found in the history of parliamentary proceedings in recent years. What is the modern rule with regard to responsibility of the government? Let me quote from Mr. Low's well known work on the ' Governance of England,' published in 1904:
That the ministry should initiate legislation is a characteristic part of our system. The cabinet drafts its measures and submits them to the legislature, which considers and discusses them, as a body, of persons arranged in parties, not as a collection of individuals, each entitled to have his own opinion on public policy and allowed some opportunity of carrying, his views into effect. Every transaction, every project of law, comes before the House as an act of the ministry and an act of the party. If it fails, or should be condemned, the result is a blow to the executive, and indirectly to that portion of the electorate by whom they are appointed. The system checks irresponsible sciolism, and hasty experimentalizing. It may render legislation slow, but it prevents it from becoming fantastic.
Further on he quotes the language of John Stuart Mill, which it may be worth while for me to quote also:
When, said John Stuart Mill, in a speech in the House of Commons in 1863, a popular body knows what it is fit for and what it is unfit for, it will mor(e and more understand that it is not its business to administer, but that it is its business to see that the administration is done by proper persons, and to keep them to their duties. I hope it will he more and more felt that the duty of this House is to put the right persons on the treasury benches, and when there to keep them to their work. People will more value the importance of this principle the longer they have experience of it.
Then the author continues as follows:
The operation of the principle has been carried much further since Mill spoke. It is not merely a question of cabinet initiative and direction, but of cabinet authority over legislation, almost unrestrained.
That is the modern doctrine in Great Britain, it is the modern doctrine in Canada. Yet, we see the government of this country, in respect to a matter of vital importance to the public welfare, abdicating its functions, interrupting the business of parliament, while allowing this debate to go on entirely irrespective of government responsibility. I eould quote further from this book in support of that principle.
I will also quote from Mr. Todd's book in support of the same principle. In Mr Todd's well known work on Parliamentary Government in England, he says, on page 500. volume 2:
It has been shown that whereas, by modern constitutional practice ministers are required to initiate Bills upon all questions affecting the public welfare-it being in the power of private members likewise to introduce similar measures-it is customary and expedient that considerable latitude should be granted to the legislative chambers in amending or rejecting the ministerial measures, without it being assumed by any such proceeding that they have withdrawn their confidence in the advisers of the Crown.
Then, further on:
But we find no example of any Bill being permitted to pass through both Houses to which ministers were persistently opposed. Where the opinion of parliament has been unequivocally expressed in favour of a particular Bill, regardless of objections thereto expressed by ministers, it has been the invariable practice for ministers either to relinquish their opposition in deference to that opinion, and to lend their aid to carry the measure, with such amendments as might he necessary to conform it to their own ideas of public policy, or else to resign.
That is the doctrine whicn Todd has laid down with regard to ministerial responsibility. But to-day we have the peculiar spectacle of this Bill presented to parliament, not upon the responsibility of the government, but upon the responsibility of a private member on the government side, and the business of the government, at this late stage of the session, being interrupted for two days. We also find the Minister of Justice rising in his place and saying that in his opinion, he being the law officer of the Crown, this Bill so presented is absolutely extreme, and one which ought not to receive the sanction of this parliament. I say again that I know of no parallel to this situation in recent years in the parliament of any English-speaking country, now, with regard to the first section of the Bill with which we are engaged at present, I do not find that it differs very much from the section in the Criminal Code of Canada as it exists today. There are two or three words omitted in different parts of the section, and I am not aware of what is supposed to be the effect of the omission of those words. We

are at this moment not doing the ordinary work done in committee of this House upon the Bill-I am not finding fault with that, I find no fault with the character of the discussion, and have no desire to interrupt it. But I do say that we must get down to business upon this section, and get through with it. I would like to find out, for my own information, what is the effect of the proposed change. At present I see no great objection to it. When we get to the other clauses of the Bill, I shall have something to say as to the effect, which, in my opinion, they would have. But I repeat that I see no great objection to this section. Nevertheless, I do say that in respect to this the whole Bill from beginning to end, it is the duty of the government to accept responsibility for this legislation, to say either that it is good legislation or that it is not good legislation, to accept full responsibility, and not run away from it as they have been doing.
Sir WILFRID LAUR1ER. My hon. friend has laid down a doctrine which he would find some difficulty in maintaining in practice in this parliament, The question which he has brought up to-day is not at all new tc old members of the House. Again and again private members have used the privilege they have of introducing legislation, and again and again the government have refused to take up a position either for or against it. If the Bill at present before us is of such a character that it is the duty of the_ government to take a position upon it, it is equally the duty of the opposition to take one side or the, other in regard to it; and if the government is failing in its duty, the opposition is equally failing in its duty. I remember many occasions in former years when legislation for a prohibitory law was introduced into this House, session after session, and the government then led by Sir John A. Macdonald always refused to take the measure up as a government measure. Old members of this House remember that very well. I see before me now men who, at that time, were members of the government, and others who were supporters of the government, and they well remember the cases to which I allude. Here is a question which interests certain members of the community. here is a question as to which men have strong views, and would like this legislation to be assumed by the government. The government, I may say-I am revealing no secret, it is a matter'of public notoriety-the government was approached and asked to make this Bill a government measure, they urged that it was of such an important character as that the government should take a position upon it. The House is aware, and the country is aware, that the government refused to [DOT] Mr R. L. BORDEN.
assume responsibility for the measure, the government refused to take it up. But while the government were of that opinion, men who were promoting this legislation thought that they would use the privilege which is given to every member of this House to present Bills for the consideration of the House. Those men have strong views upon moral questions, and regarded this question as of great importance, and it was the duty of the government to give them an opportunity of presenting their views to the House in regard to it. This opportunity has been given them by the government and having given them that opportunity the government have discharged their duty and are not called upon to do anything more. If my hon. friend thinks that v'e are bound to have an attitude upon this question I will say to him that I have known instances in which my hon. friend has introduced resolutions stating that it was our duty to introduce legislation of such and such a character. I remember that not more than three or four years ago, my hon. friend, in his official capacity in this House as leader of the opposition, introduced a resolution to the effect that it was the duty of the government to take up such and such a question with reference to the electoral law. Then, my hon. friend thought it was a question of such importance that, in the language of the authority which he has just quoted, the government were bound to take a position and to say whether they were or were not in favour of his Bill to amend the electoral law. His position is to-day that it is the duty of the government to announce a policy upon this particular; question. But, it must be remembered that the country at large has not yet formed an opinion upon this question. We know liow in British countries reforms are generally carried out. It does no^ follow that that which is taken to be public opinion will turn out to be a reform. Very often questions are brought up and finally the change is accepted as a reform. We know how many years it took to bring about the great reforms of the last century not only in this country but in Great Britain, and we know how long a time elapsed before they were taken up by the government. Let me take a famous instance, an instance with which we are all familiar-the abolition of the Corn laws. How many, years did it take? How many times was that Bill introduced before it was taken up by the government? ' Was it the first, the second or the third year? No, it was not until five, or six, or if I mistake not ten years had elapsed that public opinion had been brought to that pitch of excitement, to that degre.e of conviction, that the government thought there was need of re-

form, that there was a question to be determined and then they put their hands to the plough and carried out that great reform. My hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) has brought the attention of the House to this question. It is the first time, in so far as my memory goes, that it has ever come before the Canadian people. There have been petitions presented in favour of it. I have not heard of any counter opinion but the opinion of men is not formed upon it. Some are for it and some are against it. On this, side of the House some are for it and some are against it; on the other side of the House, some are for it and some are against it. I say to my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) that whatever may the case in the future, at the present time public opinion has not reached such a point that the government feel called upon to take an attitude upon this question. It is a free question and so it ought to remain notwithstanding that my hon. friend thinks that it is the duty of the government to take it up.
I would like to ask my right hon. friend if he thinks there is an evil which requires to be reformed?

As far as the government is concerned.

Is there an evil in respect to the matter brought before the House which requires to be reformed?
