I think there is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In that respect my hon. friend and 1 are alike; I think there is an evil which we should make an effort to reform.
May I be permitted to say to my hon. friend that if there is an evil that the government thinks requires a remedy why does not the government take the responsibility of remedying it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend, has misquoted what I said; I did not say there was an evil which the government thought should be reformed. He has turned my sentence to serve his own purpose. I said there was an evil which I thought should be reformed, but the hon. gentleman has turned the sentence in order that he could serve his own purpose. I am sorry that the only contribution which the hon. gentleman could make to this debate is 209
'a miserable effort to make party capital out of it. I dissent entirely from the extreme to which the hon. gentleman presses the doctrine that the government are responsible for every measure that comes before the House. If it were so we might have to lay down a new doctrine, and say that the hon. gentleman has as much responsibility as we have in this matter. The hon. gentleman presses the doctrine that the government must take up every question that comes before the House, and he asks for precedents. My right hon. friend the leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has given him precedents in the history of this country, and these are certainly more to our purpose than precedents drawn even from the British parliament. I am sure that every member of this House, the older members, and even those who are not old members, can recall cases where questions arose in this House on which the members of the government differed. If they differ, which is the better course-that they should pretend to agree or that they should frankly say: This is not a party question, this "is not a government question, it is a question upon which members of the government disagree, and therefore, we propose to leave it an open question before the House. There is this curious thing that when it comes to a public Bill, or a private Bill, or anything which is in the nature of a Bill, if it so happens that the members of the government unite upon the matter, we are instantly told from the other side of the House that the party whip is being used. That is the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite. When it happens accidentally that a number of the members of the government think alike, and apeak in support of a private Bill, the cry is raised that it is not a government measure, and that we are being brought into line by the party whip. If the facts had been as represented the criticism would be just. Our system of party government calls for unity of action in a great many things, but in all things it is not possible to have unity, and if, in this matter, there be differences of opinion among members of the government surely the most sensible thing is that we should say to my hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller): You have brought an important question before the House, we do not all agree on it, let it be an open question, and let each man vote as he thinks best. My right hon. friend cited one of the precedents in Great Britain for the position which he takes. If you look for them I am sure you could see other precedents of the same kind. I have a precedent in my mind that occurred not long ago, the question of Women's suffrage. The question of the right to vote is at least as important a question as that which is dealt with in this Bill



before the House. But do we not all know that the British government have declined to take ground upon that suffrage question? A member of the British government stated at a great public meeting that there was a division of opinion in the House, and in both parties on that great question, and that the government were not prepared to take the responsibility of a' woman's, suffrage Bill. He said that if a woman suffrage Bill was brought before the House, and a majority of the House would vote for it, then the government would recognize it to be its duty to take it up, and give effect to the will of the House, but that up to that time the government was not prepared to act. Is that violating all the traditions of the British parliament? I say that the extreme to which my hon. friend has pressed the matter is not warranted. It is not in accordance with the best practice of the British parliament, and I take the ground that it is not consistent with common sense. If upon any question, not a matter of vital importance, in the view of all the members of the government, there is a difference of opinion which prevents the government uniting, and coming to this House with a measure, the simple common sense method is to say:	This is a fair,
open matter for debate, and each one of us shall vote in accordance with his judgment, so that the will of the House shall be allowed to prevail.
The doctrine laid down by the Minister of Finance is a new one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at all, it is very old; my hon. friend has practised it. .

The doctrine as practised in this House, and as I have heard the Prime Minister state on former occasions is that the government is responsible for all legislation, private or other wise. There is no doubt as to the responsibility,, and there is no doubt that the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) is right in saying that the government are responsible for all measures which pass this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is where they recommend the Royal Assent to them.

Not when they represent the Royal Assent, the government is responsible for the legislation that passes this House. That is the doctrine that has always been held in the House. There is no objection to an hon. gentleman introducing a Bill, and discussing it, but when a public Bill refers to crime, and a minister of the cabinet ridicules the idea of it being a crime, and says that such an absurdity was never heard of, I have only to say that if there is one thing for which the cabinet ought to be responsible it is the definition Mr. FIELDING.
of what is a crime. These gentlemen are capable of holding different opinions upon such subjects. They say it is a duty and privilege of the government for a member of the government, the Minister of Justice, to declare that what the Bill proposes to make a crime is ridiculous, and for these gentlemen to hold different opinions. In England it is impossible for a private individual to pass a Bill, that can only be done by the consent of the government. He may introduce a Bill, and. discuss it perhaps for several sessions, he may impose his opinions on the House, those opinions, may be forced on the government, and the government may introduce the Bill. A Bill of this kind 'could not become law in England without the government consenting to it, and taking it up. I contend that the principle laid down by the leader of the. oppo-tion is the correct one, that the government is responsible for all legislation, be it a railway Bill, or any other Bill. They have no right to have differences of opinion on a question coming before the House. Ministers may have different opinions, but when it comes to legislation they ought to have but one opinion, each measure should have the unanimous support of the government. I should judge from the speech of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that he has heard the opinions of the gentleman who has introduced this Bill, and the arguments on the subject, but does hot intend to let it become law until they have had further opportunity of discussing it, that the government have not formed an opinion on the subject. That is perfectly proper, they have a right to say that. The question has been discussed in this House, they have not come to a conclusion on the subject, but they ought to be prepared to say whether legislation of that kind shall be permitted, and receive the government sanction.

The leader of the opposition has spoken of the differences between section 226 in the Bill, and in the Criminal Code as it is to-day. That hon. gentleman has said that he had no objection to section 226 as it is in the proposed Bill, but that he would like to know the meaning of the changes that have been made. He will notice that in every place where the words ' a place ' are used in the present section in the Code, the words ' house, room, or other place ' are used. The words ' a house or room ' have been left out.
What is the object?

It was held by the courts that the U3e of the words ' a house or room ' rather weakened than strengthened the language, and therefore the words were left out, leaving simply the word ' place ' and in the next section a definition of the word ' place * has been inserted. That is supposed to strengthen the language.

I understand then that the _ courts have held that the word ' place ' in the law as it is to-day must be construed with reference to the words ' house or room ' and therefore that the meaning of the word ' place ' is not.so wide in connection with these two words as it would be if it wa3 there alone.

Yes. The great opposition of the Minister of Justice was because the Bill interfered with private betting. I propose when we come to section 2 to add:
The provision of this section shall not extend to the case of a bet between individuals neither of whom is engaged in book-making or betting as a business.
And if the Minister of Justice will say when we come to consider section ^35 that it is necessary to add these words to that section I will be willing to do it so "that it will be clear that the Bill does not interfere with private betting.

Before the House rose for dinner, some discussion had taken place with regard to the functions of an opposition on matters of public importance coming before a government. The hon. Finance Minister asked the opinion of the leader of the opposition, and the right hon. the Prime Minister stated that if it were important that the government should adopt a policy with regard to a public Bill of this kind, it was also important that the opposition should do likewise. I would like to refer the right hon. gentleman to a statement made by Edmund Burke in his speech on Conciliation with America, in which he laid down what he conceived to be the duties of an opposition. He said:
It generally argues some degree of natural impotence of mind or some want of knowledge of the world to hazard plans of government except from the seat of authority.
And I have no doubt that when hon. gentlemen on this side of the House cross to the other side, they will not shirk their responsibility with regard to public Bills, as is being done with regard to this particular Bill. Before hon. members come to a conclusion with regard to this measure, I would like that there should be no misapprehension in their minds with regard to the Bill and the amendment. The hon. Minister of Justice, who should be greatly concerned with this Bill, which if it passes will become part of the criminal law of the country, takes up section 227 of the Bill, and reads it as follows :
A common betting place is a place-
(a) used for the purpose of betting between persons resorting thereto and 209*
(ii) any person using the same.
And he says that if a gentleman went to a horse race accompanied by a fair companion and laid a wager with her of a pair of gloves, it would not be a long cry for a magistrate to find him guilty under this Act. Now, I would like to point out to hon. members that it is essential that there be two parties to a bet, and this Act fixes as one of the parties ' persons resorting thereto,' that is, to the race-track, and the other party, as ' the owner, occupier or keeper thereof,' or ' any person using the same.' The Minister of Justice wishes to draw the inference that the ' persons resorting thereto ' are 'users ' of the place. They are not within the meaning of this Act, because the user of a place undoubtedly means the lessee or tenant or some one occupying the race-track. I submit that it is straining a criminal enactment beyond the limits that any court would strain it, in order to put the interpretation on this section that the Minister of Justice does. He was straining at a gnat when he sought to convey the idea that a person would be convicted who would bet a pair of gloves at a horse race. There is absolutely nothing in this Bill which would make a person liable for private betting at a race-track or outside of a race-track. But, says the Minister of Justice, I am opposed to the Bill, and I am in favour of the amendment. We find how he strained at a gnat; let us see how he can swallow a camel. Subsection 4 of section 228A of the amendment reads as follows:
4- Dor the purpose of this section the word
street ' shall include any highway and any public bridge, road, lane, footway, square, court, alley or passage, whether a thoroughfare or not; and the words 'public place' shall include public park, garden, or sea-beach, and any uninclosed ground to which the public for the time being have restricted access, and shall also include every inclosed place (not being a public park or garden) to which the public have a restricted right of access, whether on payment or otherwise, if at or near every public entrance there is conspicuously exhibited by the owners or persons having control of the place a notice prohibiting betting therein.
Now, I would like hon. members to keep that paragraph of the amendment in mind. In effect, it operates in this way. A is the owner of a race-track. B is a book-maker. B goes to A and says: ' I would like to make a book at your race-track next week.' A says: 'What will you give me?' B says: 'I will give you 25 per cent.' A says:	'That is not sufficient.' 'Well,'
says B, * I will make my book outside of your race-track.' A says: 'No, indeed, you will not, because I will put up notices prohibiting betting.' ' Then,' says B, ' well, what do you want? ' A says: 'I want 50 per cent.' ' Well,' says B, ' if you must

have 50 per cent, I will give it. A says:
' All right, walk right in, make yourself comfortable, go on with your betting, there will be no signs put up '; and the betting goes merrily on. I venture to say that if the members of the jockey club from whom this amendment emanates had prepared it last summer and presented it to this House this winter, they would not have got ten members -of this House on either side to support it. It simply means placing in the hands of the owners of race-track and gambling resorts the authority to make it legal or" illegal to gamble, according to their own fancy. When this Bill was up for its second reading, the Minister of Justice, poking some fun at the definition of a betting place in the Act, cracked what he considered to be a very good conundrum. He asked:	' When is a dog's tail not a
dog's tail ? The answer was: ' When it is a-waggin'; and he thought it a very good joke. Well, I would like to say that in this subsection 4 there also arises a conundrum. It is: ' When is an offence not an offence'? The answer is: ' When there is no notice on the fence.' Now, this amendment, vesting the right to say that gambling may or may not be carried on, in the owner's and lessees of race-tracks is one of the most flagrant and barefaced pieces of legislation ever offered to a legislative body. It is an insult to this parliament to ask it to legislate in that way. I wish the hon. members of this House, before voting on this Bill, to bear in mind that the Bill as it now stands before the committee does not interfere *with private betting, and that the amendment as proposed clothes the owners and lessees of race-tracks with authority to say whether gambling shall be carried on legally or not, which would be a lamentable state of affairs.
Some hon. MEMBEES. Question, question.

I want to say a word or two as to the opinion given by the Minister of Justice before dinner in regard to the section of the Bill we are now discussing, and in regard to the amendment. The hon. the Minister of Justice says he prefers the amendment offered by the hon. member for West Northumberland (Mr. McColl) to the Bill as it is before the House. Let me call the attention of the committee to the last paragraph of the amendment:
Provided no such race-meeting shall continue for more than 12 days of continuous racing.
The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) said he thought that would, be a great improvement. I would like to ask where the improvement is in narrowing racing to twelve days per meeting and allowing two meetings in a year.
It is eight days in the amendment, not twelve.	*

That would make it 16 days in the year. It would cut four days off the Woodbine meet as held to-day. It would be an improvement, not to those who are supporting the Bill, but to the proprietors of race-track associations in this way. The law, as interpreted by Canadian courts, compels a book-maker to move about from place to place and prohibits him from locating himself anywhere; but if we pass this amendment, the book-maker will be able to do business as before and be made as comfortable as possible on the racetrack. What I want to get at is the legal aspect of the case, and I would like to compare the amendment offered by the hon. member for West Northumberland (Mb. McColl), and advocated by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth), with the written opinion of the Minister of Justice as given on the 5th of February.

As the hon. gentleman has mentioned my name, I think the committee should understand my position. I did not say, and I am not concerned in saying, whether we are injuring race-track men or not, I am not anxious to injure anybody by this legislation, and I do not think it was wise for the hon. gentleman to support the Bill by saying that it is handicapping race-track associations. What I did say was that if we confined betting to the race-tracks and absolutely prohibited it outside, we would make a great advance and limit the character and the amount of betting.

I have no feeling against anybody, and no desire to injure any one. As I have said, I do not want to do anybody an injury, but I do not want to extend the privileges of race-track associations under the colour of advancement in the way of moral reform. The hon. the Minister of Justice advocates the amendment offered by the hon. member for West Northumberland (Mr. McColl), which would allow a meeting to last 8 days, but in the opinion which the hon. minister gave me on the 5th of February last he said, speaking on this point:
The Dominion parliament has no such jurisdiction, and the only way in which the Dominion parliament could deal 'with the subject is by undertaking to make it a crime to continue a race-track meeting for more than some given number of days.
That is what the amendment seeks to do. It seeks to make a crime on the ninth day what is perfectly legal on the other eighti,
I do not question the power of the Dominion parliament to legislate in that manner, but it certainly would seem to me entirely illogical to do so. ,
The hon. minister explained all that to-day.

What I contend is that if it was entirely illogical to do that on the 5th of February, 1910, it is just as illogical to do it on the 7th of April. I submitted the language of this Bill to the Minister of Justice. I did so in perfect frankness, and no doubt his reply was equally frank. 1 said I wanted his opinion in order that I might use it, and it was with that understanding the opinion was obtained. When I submitted the Bill to my hon. friend, he said he did not think it was his duty, as Minister of Justice, to give his opinion on a public Bill submitted by a private member, but he said that the Bill had been drafted by three most able lawyers, that they had given a great deal of thought and time to its drafting, and that it was admirably drawn. I said to the hon. minister: Do you think any other language could be used which could better carry out the purpose of its promoters. He said he did not. Referring to section 227, he thought it possible that two men sitting on adjoining seat on the grand stand and making a bet, the one with the other, might be held under this Bill to have been keeping a betting place. I said: Do you not think the language would have to be very much strained indeed to come to that conclusion? He replied: Candidly I do think it -would, but no one could tell to what extent a magistrate might strain the language of the statute. Speaking of section 235 he said there was absolutely nothing in it to interfere with private betting, although there -was something in it which would prevent the recording or registering of a private bet. I have here an amendment which I propose to offer to section 227:
The provisions of this section shall not extend to the case of a bet between individuals neither of whom is engaged in any way in book-making or in betting as a business.
If the hon. the Minister of Justice, or the majority of the committee, think that in order to protect the private bettor- whom I do not want to injure-some amendment should be attached to section 235, I am perfectly willing that the one I have just read should be. I want again to call the attention of the committee to this fact that if they carry the amendment offered by the hon. member for West Northumberland (Mr. McColl), they will be throwing the law wider open and give greater opportunity for the carrying on of professional gambling. If the condition is bad to-day, it would he a great deal worse under the amendment.
On the race-track?
Yes, it -would increase the amount of betting on the race-track.
Nowhere else?
Again I appeal to my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), with whom I am sometimes able to agree, and who sometimes has a logical mind
I have lucid intervals.
I am glad of that, because I think I will have his support.
I think the hon. gentleman had better get a lucid interval too.

The hon. member for Lincoln will not be able to give any satisfactory reply, just as every other opponent of the Bill, to this question. If it be right and proper to punish and prohibit professional gambling, by what logic can you determine it is quite right to do on a racetrack what, by the Criminal Code of Canada, is a crime every place off the racetrack? If a thing is a crime on this side of the fence, how can you make it innocent on the other side? I would like the hon. member for Lincoln to answer that.

Candidly, we have been too long talking on this subject. I would ask my hon. friend which position is the most logical, what I said two or three times to-day about limiting gambling, or his own suggestion that every individual can bet all he has, and all his family has* and do it under the name of private betting? The race-track association controls it, and limits it, and makes it less objectionable than would be an unrestricted amount of private betting. He is throwing everything wide open.

One word in answer to my hon. friend. He asks why we should prohibit what be calls gambling off the track, and permit it on the race-track. Now, if my hon. friend had heard the proceedings before the special committee and the arguments made before the House, he would have known that the conditions on the race-track and the conditions off the race-track are entirely different. When men are betting off the race-track they see no racing, there is no sport connected with it, it is gambling pure and simple. But what takes place on the race-track is altogether different. In the lirst place, the parties who go there and who patronize it are a different class of people, they are not gamblers in any sense; they go there to enjoy the races, to enjoy the sport, and the betting that they do is only an incident of the snort. Whether that Incident is right or wrong, it is something that has grown up in Great Britain for hundreds of years. As I said before, the men who patronize races in my own constituency never bet on hockey matches or anything else, never plav cards for money, but they go there to enjoy the sport, and as an in-

cident they may bet two or three dollars on a race. That is no gambling at all, and that is all that is done by nine-tenths of the people who patronize a well conducted race-track such as the Woodbine or the other tracks referred to. Moreover, the betting that takes, place on the race-track with the book-maker is done under regulations. The association regulates the bookmaker, sees that everything is done fairly, and takes every means to protect the public, and that cannot in any sense of the word be called gambling.
One point further. You, Mr. Chairman, intimated this afternoon that the amendment before the chair, and which I offered last evening before the House adjourned, was not strictly in order. If that should turn out to be the case, then, before the motion is put, I would desire to move another amendment and put it in another form, clause by clause, which I suppose would be without doubt in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The amendment moved by the hon. member was ruled out of order, there is, therefore, no amendment before the committee.

I understood, also, that you suggested this afternoon that, although it was, strictly speaking, out of order, the House had full jurisdiction over its own rules, and that if the House would like to vote upon my amendment, or the provisions of the substituted Bill, it would be at liberty to do so. If that is not out of order, I would like the feeling of the House upon it. I may say, further, that it would simplify matters and shorten proceedings a great deal if a vote could be taken in the way I have suggested. In the first place, this amendment was moved last evening before the House adjourned, and if it was out of order the question should have been raised then. It was not raised then, and we have proceeded to-day, speaking presumably upon the amendment that I had moved. If there is any technical objection to that, it might be waived and we might take a vote.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment moved by the hon. member was discussed at some length. I intimated to him some time before I did to the committee that I did not think it in order. Eventually, I stated that I did not think I could submit it to the committee. Having been ruled out of order, it was open to any hon. gentleman to question the ruling of the Chairman, but that was not done. The rule of the House I think is quite clear. The House itself can change its rules. I do not think that the Committee of the Whole House change those rules, although I would hesitate to place myself in opposition to the unanimous de-Mr. McCOLL.
sire of the committee in its method of carrying on business. However, the proposed amendment was ruled out of order, and I do not see my way clear to take the vote the hon. member speaks of. Any amendment he desires to offer to section 1 will now be in order.

(Translation). Mr. Chairman, I move that you now leave the chair. I will indicate with a few words the reason of my motion. I will not be long and I hope that some of my hon. colleagues in this House, who have the privilege of speaking both languages, will be able to express better than I can do, the motives which we can appeal to, in favour of my question.
The Bill which we are discussing now provides some qiodifications to the criminal law. For my part, I think that in such a circumstance, when an hon. member moves for a change in the criminal law, he should prove that his resolution is not intended to create an offence or to be in contradiction with a law already in force. Now, without mentioning any of the provinces of confederation, 1 can declare positively that in some provinces, what this Bill really asks for punishment is not supposed to be an offence. There are some provinces where the facts which they want to punish as criminal ones are not even an offence. For this reason, I think it would be wise for the House to send back this Bill to the provincial legislature which would discuss, reject or pass it. I consider that the question now discussed is pertinent to the civil code of Canada, Now, there are provinces that have an exclusive jurisdiction that can alone decide on matters concerning civil code. Furthermore, some provinces have an exclusive jurisdiction _ to decide upon the rights which,are pertinent to citizens to dispose of their estates. their money, and of all they own. I will insist no more. I hope we have in this House some representatives more competent than myself to make it understood by the majority that these reasons are sufficient to ask for the postponement of this Bill. I will content myself with these few remarks which I think are sufficient to justify you, Mr. Chairman, for leaving the Chair.
What is your proposition?
That Mr. Chairman do now leave the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As I understand, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roy) moves that the Chairman do now leave the Chair.

In view of the ruling which you have made I will move that section 1 of the Bill be struck out. In tak-

ing the sense of the House on that question, we shall probably have an expression upon the whole of my amendment. We have had that fully discussed, and I think the House understands now why I am put in the position of having to take this course. Section 1 of the Bill now before us reads as follows:
1. Section 226 of the Criminal Code, chapter 146 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, is repealed and the following; is substituted therefor:-
Thus, section 1 repeals section 226 of the Criminal Code, and substitutes another section. The effect of my motion to strike out this section No. 1 is to leave section 226 of the Criminal Code as it now stands. When we compare this section of the Criminal Code with the section as proposed in this Bill, we find that there is very little difference. That was fully explained this afternoon by the Minister of Justice. Section 226 as it now stands provides:
A common gambling house is-
(a)	a house, room or place kept by any person for gain, to which persons resort for the purpose of playing at any game of chance or at any mixed game of chance and skill; or
(b)	a house, room or place kept or used for
playing therein at any game of chance or any mixed game of chance and skill, in which a hank is kept by one or more of the players

and so on. About the only difference between the present section of the Criminal Code, and the section proposed by this Bill is the elimination of the expressions * house/ -and ' room,' leaving only the expression ' place.' The reason the promoters of the Bill have desired to have only 'place' in the section is to give it an extended definition making unnecessary the use of other expressions. The Bill I propose, defines ' street,' and the same thing is effected. So the two Bills are, in that respect, practically the same. Without further explanation I move to strike out section 1.

Section 1 I consider a very essential section of this Bill, in fact it is necessary to correct the present confused state of the law. It will be known to hon. members who have studied this question that the law on this point is at present in a very unsatisfactory state. The decisions of the court have been to the effect that one is liable to fine, -and imprisonment if the book-maker does.his' betting at any particular place-if, for instance, he stands on a box or under an umbrella at the race-course; but, if he walks about the race-course, or even, marks time, his betting is not an offence. This arises from the peculiar construction given by the courts to the word * place.' It was pointed out to the committee in the investigation that in the butcher shops, barber shops-, and other places in Toronto, it is a common
practice to carry on this race-course betting as a side show to the regular business. It was also shown that when a man carrying on this practice wished to escape liability, under the law he stepped out on the sidewalk, and there made the bet with his customer. The butcher, so long as he remains in his shop and makes a bet. becomes liable to -a fine, but if he stands on the sidewalk in carrying on this transaction he is not liable under the law. And, the book-maker on the race-course, while he moves -about, or even while he marks time may make a bet that is not an offence, but, standing in one place, he is liable to prosecution. I am sure every hon. member ,of this House wishes to have that state of the law corrected. The section that my hon. friend from West Northumberland (Mr. McColl) wishes t-o strike out is an attempt, and, I think, a fairly good attempt, to define what a ' place ' is and to correct that anomalous condition of the law. This does not deal with the main portion of the Bill which we reach later on, and which deals with the question whether betting by the book-maker should be allowed. I therefore trust that hon. members will look carefully into this question before voting. I can well see how hon. gentlemen who are opposed to doing away with the book-maker might vote against the motion of my hon. friend from West Northumberland to strike out this section.

I think the hon. Minister of Justice fully answered all that has been said by the member for Guvsborough (Mr. Sinclair), I understand him to say- and I quite agree with him-that the evil consists in what is done not in where it is done. As he pointed out, the first section as it stands means that persons sitting side by side are in a * place,' and if they make a private bet they are liable to be sent to jail.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the difficulty I feel with regard to the situation, arises, perhaps, from the ruling which, I understand, you have made, that the amendment which was moved by the hon. member for West Northumberland (Mr. McColl is not iji order. The difficulty in dealing with this section arises from the fact that the various sections of the English Bill which the hon. member for West Northumberland moved en bloc by way of amendment last night are so in-terwoven, so interdependent one upon the other that, unless- you are to consider them all together, you are scarcely in a -position to deal intelligently with the matter. The difficulty which my hon. friend from Guys-borough has pointed out with regard to what he considers the anomalous condition of the law is, I venture to think, nothing of the sort The law was perfect! r

clear, and distinct as it left this House in 1892. The House then, in terms, decided to except from the book-making prohibition if you please, to except from the betting clause of the Criminal Code, a number of things, among which were bets made on the race-course of an incorporated association during the actual progress of a racemeeting. But the wording of the exception limited the exception to that particular clause. The wording of the exception was and is:
The provisions of this section shall not extend to bets made on a race-track during a race-meeting.
Accordingly the law did not prevent a book-maker from making a book on a race-track during the progress of a race-meeting, but that condition of the law did not please the people who want to stop book-making, and accordingly they resorted to a prosecution of the book-maker under this other section for keeping a betting house, to which other section the exception did not, in terms, apply. They procured in that way a fine or conviction to be imposed upon some book-maker, notwithstanding that he had made his bets upon a race-track during a race-meeting, upon the theory that because he stood upon a box or under an umbrella, he was thereby keeping a common betting house. The section dealing with a gaming house is another section of similar character to the section that deals with a betting house, and the proposal now before the committee simply resolves itself into this form. Whereas the existing law, section 226, defines a common gaming house to be a house, room or place,' &c., the amending section which the committee has reported and recommended, proposes to change the phraseology from the words ' gaming house ' to the words ' gaming place,' and instead of calling it a ' house, room or place kept by a person,' &c., it is now to he called a ' place used by a person,' so that it will not necessarily be an inclosure_ at all. but in the language of fhe definition, which, by the next section, it is proposed to apply to this section under consideration, fhe word ' place ' is to include ' any place whether' inclosed or not and whether it is used permanently or temporarily and whether there is or is not the exclusive right of user.' In voting upon this proposition, hon. gentlemen should understand that what they are doing is Teally taking that integral portion of the proposal submitted or reported by the committee with the idea of changing the existing law in order to make ' common gaming house ' or ' common gaming place ' something that is not inclosed, or stationary, or permanently or exclusively used, but something "which is, as it were, just a step toward what I spoke of this after-Mr. AYLESWORTH.
noon, that is getting after the individual bettor if he makes a bet when he is sitting on his seat.

I am not anxious to detain the House, but I do not feel like giving a silent vote. I had not intended taking part in this discussion, but some incidents that occurred just before six o'clock impel me to give the reasons for the faith that is in me, a faith that has been seriously deepened by the remarks of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Ayles-worth). As far as the amendemnt proposed by the hon. member for West Northumber-lan (Mr. McColl) is concerned, its adoption would practically mean the voting down of the Bill. His amendment must be regarded as a crucial matter, as the Minister of Justice explains that while the provisions of the old criminal law are for getting after the gambler or the criminal who breaks the law in every place except at a race-track meeting, the object of the amendment to the Criminal Code proposed to the Bill introduced by the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) means to go after the professional gambler wherever he is and, if possible, stamp him cut of existence. That, as far as I understand it, is the general principle involved. I think we all thoroughly understand that we are loath 1o be beaten into virtue by legislative enactment. We do not believe that a legislative enactment can improve our moral standpoint or make men law-abiding citizens. It must also be understood that to a great many men, and myself amongst them, race-track gambling and betting have no particular temptation, and we must be all the more careful as we may have other forms of temptation not to
Compound for sins we are'inclined to
By damning those we have no mind to.
We ought, at all events, to give fair play to the gentlemen who are in sympathy with the amendment proposed by the hon. member for West Northumberland. The strongest speeches I heard, in following this debate, against this proposed amendment to the law were made b,y the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sift-on) and the hon. Minister of Justice. The hon. member for Brandon stated that his principal reasons-and we ought to give them all due weight, were these: First of all, that the matter had not been threshed out before the country. I might deal with that very briefly. I do not think that he -can put that argument forward very seriously. As was pointed out, there never has been an amendment to the Criminal Code that has ever been threshed out before the country. I might retort to my hon. friend the member for Brandon that a great, many matters that this government have incorporated into law have not been threshed out before the country, namely, the Autonomy Bill, the

Grand Trunk Pacific Railway (Bill, the Naval Bill. The country never had an opportunity of saying a word in Tegard to these measures. He also introduced an argument with which I had more sympathy, and that was that the passage of laws with which a preponderating part of the public were not in active sympathy only tended to increase the general contempt for law. That argument has a great deal ol weight. But the hon. member for Brandon pushed his argument to the farthest point, and he did admit that there were a great many evils-he numbered them as four, all of which meant betting and gambling in various forms, and he assented to the fact that these were evils that ought to be stamped out. But, I was rather astonished that he could not carry his argument to its logical conclusion and assent also to the necessity of stamping out the fifth, namely, that which, is a legalization of gambling on the race-track. Let me deal with another phase of the amendment with regard to the first part of the Bill and with the important principle involved in the Bill. I feel that whether we gamble on races or do not we have to deal *with these questions as citizens of a great country, and as men interested in progress along the best lines in every community, and we must admit that gambling and betting, carried on as they are in that form, are provocative of a great many evils leading directly to cheating, unfair play of various kinds, and even to worse and more nefarious practices.
I d'o not say they always lead to these evils, but I do say, and I think the House will agree, that wholesale and legalized gambling on race-tracks does not foster the best spirit of sport. That while those who love sport for sport's sake would do nothing unfair, men to whom the love of sport is entirely subordinate to the love of gain would take a more active part in connection with these races, and I say there is thus an influence at -work leading to cheating, unfair play, pulling races, etc. Indirectly it leads to graver evils, such as embezzlement, forgery, debt, etc. I believe at all events, and this is my reason for voting, that gambling and betting in any way to a certain extent, but certainly in a large and professional way, is anti-social in its influence, that is, it does not tend to a healthy constructive progress in _ a community, but rather tends to its disintegration. The hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) stated before six o'clock that he thought the government ought to accept some responsibility for a measure of this kind, and on this point he was replied to by the hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the right hon. gentleman who leads the House (Sir .Wilfrid Laurier). I thoroughly agree that the government ought to assume such responsibility, and for the reason that it is not an ordinary measure, it is not an ordinary private Bill, but a Bill that involves an amendment to the Criminal Code of Canada, 'for which surely the government must have some responsibility. The right hon. gentleman who leads this House very airily washed his hands, of any responsibility in regard to this measure. He has not told us, as I think he should have done, where he stood on this particular measure, how he viewed so important a thing as an amendment to the Criminal Code, which certainly directly concerns him. But what is the peculiar position in which the government stand? The right hon. gentleman and the Minister of Finance have said that this is a question of great gravity upon which the members of the government do not agree, and the Minister of Finance, therefore, said it would be more sensible to leave it to the judgment of the House. Certainly it would be more sensible as party tactics for the government to leave it to the House. I have always been told that the doctrine of cabinet solidarity is a very important one, one that should be taken seriously. They are throwing that to one side. What is the position if the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister or other ministers of the Crown choose to vote for the proposed Bill? We are in this position that there is an amendment to the Criminal Code which has been denounced in the strongest and, I was going to say, in the most violent, but certainly in very strong language by the chief minister of the Crown dealing with the law, the Minister of Justice. He has poured ridicule on the Bill brought in by the member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) "and he has added-and that is why I say it is the Bill, the whole Bill and nothing but the Bill-he has added that he was going to vote for an amendment which practically kills the Bill. The Minister of Justice laid stress on the fact that the gravest injury that could be done to the body politic in this whole matter was to bring in a contempt of law in general, because we were passing statutes that could not be lived up to. Let me ask the Minister of Justice what position will the country and parliament be in if members of the government like the First Minister and other ministers vote for this Bill and allow it to be carried, and it is carried in face of the fact that the Minister of Justice has condemned it as a piece of preposterous legislation which is a farce and absolutely wrong. Is that not bringing the whole law into contempt, if the chief minister of the law and the government allow a piece of legislation to go on the statute-book which they regard as farcial. I say it is bringing the law into contempt to a greater extent than anything the government have

done, and I believe that government ought to arrange a fair compromise if they can, or at all events take some steps to shoulder the responsibility of so important a measure as this.

Amendment agreed to, yeas 78, nays 77.

Mr. MeCOLL. I made the suggestion, and would like to hear the expression of the House upon it, that we vote on the whole Bill, as I first suggested. If that is not in order, I will have to move to strike out this section.

speechtext:
I do not feel any more at liberty to allow the original amendment of the hon. member for West Northumberland than I did on the previous section.
Mr. MeCOLL. Then I move to strike out this section for the same reasons and on the same grounds as I did section 1.

I desire to state why I am opposed to this section, as I am to several sections of this Bill. The law in this country relating to common gaming houses, common betting houses, and the other matters mentioned in these sections, has stood long, is in thorough accord with the traditions of English law, and has been well settled by innumerable judicial decisions. I-doubt if there are any sections of the Criminal Code as to which there

have been more litigation and more illuminating decisions than the sections relating to gambling; and the reason for the present attempt to wipe out those sections is that they do not cover cases which they were never intended to cover. That would be giving them a fantastic meaning. It is proposed to amend sections which are generally settled, wisely settled, usefully settled, as thejr stand, in order to make them cover what they were never intended to cover. If you amend them in this way, you will throw into confusion that portion of the law which is already well settled. If an amendment were introduced dealing expressly with the race-track, and dealing with it in a reasonable way, I for one would support it; but to amend the whole law on this subject merely to cover that one case, and to Convert ' a common gaming house ' or ' a common betting house ' into ' a common betting place,' terms which are not known to the law, and which we do not understand, and to give this phrase a strained and extensive meaning, is not in my opinion called for by the" state of the law on the subject, and is not in the interest of the proper restriction of gambling. It is the universal opinion of those who have studied the subject that there is great danger in gambling, and that there is wisdom is the restriction imposed by the British law which deals with gaming houses and betting houses when they become public nuisances. The British law on this as on other subjects does not deal so much with their moral aspects as with the duties and rights of men towards their fellowmen; it does not deal with this matter as a moral question, but as a question affecting the public and individual. For the reasons I have given, I intend to vote against all these amendments which propose in an uncertain and unsafe way to amend provisions of the law which are now well established and most useful in their operation.
I beg to move that the rules of this committee be amended, so that instead of taking a standing vote, we call for the yeas and nays.

I think we ought to do something with this Bill. We have spent two days upon this serious question of gambling. Let me appeal to the committee as well as to the Prime Minister that we do not waste these two days, and, while the matter is fresh in our minds, put a proper Bill on the statute-books of this country. Let us pass a Bill as suggested by the Minister of Justice which seems to be in accordance with the opinion of the majority of the House. Why should we have wasted these two days when we are here in the interest of the country to suppress this gambling evil? Why does not the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) join with the majority of the House in making the best Bill he can under the circumstances? ister, and have done nothing to put this Bill in proper shape? We can do it in twenty minutes or fifteen minutes if we concentrate our minds upon it. The contention is all over, the main points of the Bill have been settled. Let us put them into shape and let up pass this Act. Do not let the country say that we are a lot of children, and farcical children at that, spending two whole days and doing nothing.

This motion will no doubt carry, and the carrying of it will very likely result in no further action being taken on this Bill during this session. It will leave the race-tracks, the race-track owners and the race-meetings exactly in the position they have stood in hitherto. But the great question to my mind in reference to the whole proceedings is to limit the number of days on which race-meetings should be held. The amendments which have been made to the Act are really infinitesimal in their effect. The so-called Miller Bill is no more effective than the law as it stands now. What I was anxious for, and what I believe the majority of the members of this committee and this parliament are anxious for, is to have it definitely and finally settled as to how many days each year races should be held on the various race-tracks. I believe the consensus of opinion of the whole people, at any rate of Ontario, is that two meetings of twelve days each during the year are quite enough, that races should not be conducted longer than that, and I think it will be well, as this question will not come up again very likely this session, that we should tell the race-track owners and operators to take notice that unless they shorten the terms of their meetings very likely this matter will come up again next session, and be dealt with in a way that will not be to their satisfaction. I think that if section 235. as it is in the Miller Bill, had been reached it should have restricted the number of days racing and fixed definitely and finally that question for all time to come. That is the principal object of the Bill, and I think that if those people who are engaged in this legitimate sport-and it is a sport that I would like to see continued, but kept under reasonable restrictions-should take notice that long race-meetings will not be tolerated in Canada.

The whole scope of the amendment is to substitute proceedings under the Expropriation Act for proceedings under the Railway Act. This is a change which the chairman of the commission, as I understand with the concurrence of his fellow members of the commission, thinks is of very considerable importance. He came to Ottawa accompanied by the solicitor for the commission to discuss this proposal, along with some other changes which, after discussion, did not seem to be of so much importance and which have therefore not been proposed. merit, as hon. gentlemen will see, relieves the commission of these preliminary steps and requires the proceedings to fix the price for the land which has been taken against the owners will to be had in the Exchequer Court instead of before a Board of Arbitrators to be selected in accordance with the provisions of the Railway Act. The steps that are to be taken are marked out in detail in the original statute and are not interfered with. The approval of this House must first be had to the proposed transaction. Once that approval is secured, the proceedings will continue, either by agreement or by expropriation.

When this Bill was being considered before, I put a question which I repeat now, because the answer I got then, if I understood it correctly, was not satisfactory; that is, in the event of the commission requiring what is known as the Ross rifle property, which is under lease, but which belongs to the Crown, would it be expropriated, or by what means would it be taken over?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

It is proposed to raise the salaries of the post office inspectors, the assistant post office inspectors, the superintendents of railway mail clerks and certain assistant postmasters. The salaries of these officers are fixed by the Civil Service Act relating to the outside service. It has been found that this class of employees are those upon whose efficiency and industry we must chiefly rely for good administration of the department. The post office inspectors are the very marrow of the whole service. Under the Post Office Act it is their duty to:
(a)	Superintend the performance of the mail service, take good cafe that, as far as the state of the roads and other circumstances permit, the stipulations of all contracts for the conveyance of the mail are strictly complied with by the contractor.
(b)	Instruct new postmasters in their duty.
_ (c) Keen the postmasters to their duty in rendering their accounts and paying over their balances.
And so on and so on. They are, as I say, the officers on whose efficiency the whole postal service and the administration of the department depends. Their salaries have not been revised, practically, since confederation. They are at the head of the service, and I think we should give them, this year, now that times are more prosperous, some little lift. Last year, with the concurrence of the House, I gave increases to the lower grades of the service, the stampers, sorters and labourers, and this year I thought the time had come w'hen the post office inspectors, who render such ^efficient service, the assistant post office' inspectors, the superintendents of the railway mail service and the assistant postmasters in the large cities, should be receive an increase. The amount involved is not very large. There are 16 inspectors, who will receive under this Bill increases amounting to $3,300. There are 18 assistant inspectors whose increases or salary will affect our revenue to the extent of $7,850. There are 8 superintendents of the railway mail service who will receive an



aggregate increase of $750. And there are 7 assistant postmasters who will receive increases amounting to $3,000. In all, the amount involved under the present resolution is $10,800. If the House desires further explanation I shall be ready to give it.
For the sake of clearness this resolution will be included with one to be moved by my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) and made part of a Bill affecting the Civil Service, which is to be presented in a day or two by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher). So I would ask that this resolution pass and that it should stand over for further consideration until it be incorporated in the Bill to which I have referred.
The post office inspectors have not had a readjustment of their salaries for a long time?
Since 1874.

They have very important duties to perform, and, so far us I am concerned, I quite approve of these proposals.
Resolution reported, read the second time, and agreed to.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, 1907, by providing for the payment to the chairman and members of a Board of Conciliation and Investigation, of an allowance at the rate of twenty dollars for each day's sitting of the board and for each day necessarily engaged in travelling from or to their places of residence to attend or after attending a meeting of the board.-Mr. King.

This resolution Is necessary in consequence of one amendment it is proposed to make to the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. At the present time, the chairman of a board of .conciliation receives $20 a day and the other members of the board $15 a day. It has appeared that this rate of remuneration is hardly adequate for the services rendered, having regard to the payments made in arbitrations of much less important subjects than those under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, and it is suggested to change the rates of remuneration to allow all the members of the board the same rate, viz.. $20 a day. It is true that the chairman has some special duties to perform, but it has also been shown in practice that the other members of the board representing the two parties have also special services in the way of endeavouring to effect a conciliation, which Mr. LEMIEUX.
services are performed at times other than those during which the board is sitting, and for which they receive no remuneration whatever. It is thought that by allowing all the members of the board $20 per day the services of the members in this particular will be compensated.
Is th^re any difference in the qualification required from the chairman and from the other members of the board?
The members of the board are chosen in the first instance by the parties themselves, each side is given an opportunity of naming a representative.
They have not to have any special qualification-

It is left to the parties themselves to say who shall represent them. As a matter of fact, the representatives that have been chosen in the past have been almost vdthout exception men of exceptional ability.
What was the reason in the first place for making a difference in the stipend between the one as compared with the other two?

It was thought before we had any experience under the Act that probably the duties of the chairman would be more onerous than those of the other members of the board. But it has turned out that while the chairman has some duties that are not performed by the other members, the individual members have a great deal of work after hours conferring with the parties whom they represent with a view to bringing the two sides together, and their time is taken up in a manner in which the chairman's time is not.
What has been the expenditure for the enforcement of this Act during the past year?
The first year $16,000 was required, the second year $20,000, and this year the expenditure will amount to $20,000, possibly a little more.
Has the hon. gentleman before him the number of disputes that have been settled in each of the years mentioned?

The Act has now been on the statute-book for over three years. During that time there have been applications for 82 boards. In 76 cases out of the 82
settlements have been effected and strikes or lockouts averted, and in only 6 cases have the boards failed to bring about a settlement between the narties. or their findings not been accepted by one side or the other.
Is the number of applications on the increase?
During the fiscal year ended March 31 of the present year, there were 30 applications for boards.
How many in 1906?

From March 22, 1907, to March 31, 1908, there were 35 applications; in the next year there were 20, and last year 30. There have been 5 less during the last fiscal year than during the first year of the Act, and 10 more than during the second year.

I would suggest that there should he a little difference in the compensation of the ordinary member on the board and the chairman. I think that when you take a judge off the bench to act as third man, you can hardly expect him to work for less than $25 a day.

With regard to the judges, they already receive pay for their services under the regular allowance granted by parliament, and I think in their case at least there is no special reason for giving them any extra allowance. As to other persons who act in the position of chairman, I would say that the department has found no difficulty during the past in obtaining suitable persons at that remuneration.
Resolutions reported, read the second time, and agreed to.
